About this work

The Steganographia is Trithemius's most famous and most notorious work: a treatise in three books, written about 1499–1500 and circulated for a century in manuscript before it was first printed (Frankfurt, 1606). On its surface it is a manual of angel-magic — long conjurations addressed to spirit-princes and their subordinate spirits, each governing a quarter of the heavens, a wind, or an hour of the day. Beneath that surface it is a cryptographic system: the "conjurations" are cover-text, and the real message is carried by the spirit-names and the numeric keys tabulated for each prince. It was the disguise that undid him. Manuscript copies reached readers they were not meant for — Carolus Bovillus among them — who took the spirit-magic at face value and accused Trithemius of necromancy; the book was placed on the Index, and the third book's reputation as genuinely demonic persisted until its cipher was solved — first by Thomas Ernst (1996), then independently by Jim Reeds (1998). Trithemius's own answer to the charge is the Trithemius sui ipsius vindex of 1616, also in this corpus (prdl-32287).

The Latin source here is the 1621 Darmstadt edition — printed by Balthasar Aulaeander (the Latinized name of Balthasar Hofmann) at the expense of Johann Berner — recovered from the Bibliothèque nationale de France / Gallica. The work was absent from this corpus's original acquisition pass and was reassembled from its 168 IIIF page-images. It was re-OCR'd with the same vision model used across the corpus and translated by GPT-5.5 with a Fable 5 review pass against the page scans; the review recovered the cipher tables and the Early-New-High-German cover-text letters that a first pass tends to flatten into placeholders. The cipher is decoded — in a separate cryptanalysis (eleven modi, II–XI and XXXII–XXXIX, decoded by inverting each modus's printed alphabet) on the cipher solutions page. In the body translation here the Latin and its German cover-text are rendered as they stand, not decoded inline. For the cryptographic machinery see the companion Clavis texts (prdl-70281, prdl-70282), Ernst (1996) and Reeds (1998), and for the comprehensive English edition Stephen Skinner & Daniel Clark, Steganographia: Books I–IV (Llewellyn, 2024). The work ships at audit tier S after the 2026-06 dual-grader consensus established that cipher apparatus, catalogues, and honest illegible-page markers are faithful rather than hallucinated.

Steganography: The Art of Hidden Writing

[unclear]

STEGANOGRAPHIA: That is: The art, by hidden writing, of safely disclosing the will of one's mind to those who are absent; by the most reverend and most distinguished man, Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim and most perfect master of Natural Magic.

Prefixed to this work is its key, or true introduction, composed by the author himself; until now much desired by many, but seen by very few. Now, for the sake of students of the more secret philosophy, it has been made public.

With the privilege and consent of superiors.

Darmstadt. From the printing office of Balthasar Aulæandti, at the expense of Johann Berner, bookseller of Frankfurt. In the year 1621.

TO THE READER. You should be advised, candid reader, that of the letters R. and S., in this work sometimes added as numbers, sometimes as characters, sometimes as words written above on the page or added in the margin, the former denotes rubric, or red color, and the latter ink, or black color. You will also observe this: that the individual titles of the individual chapters are likewise to be painted and adorned in rubric. You may seek the significance of this matter from the Key prefixed to the work. Farewell.

HERE BEGINS THE FIRST BOOK OF THE STEGANOGRAPHY OF JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, ABBOT OF SPANHEIM, OF THE ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT, OF THE DIOCESE OF MAINZ, TO THE MOST SERENE PRINCE, LORD PHILIP, COUNT PALATINE OF THE RHINE, DUKE OF BAVARIA, AND PRINCE ELECTOR OF THE HOLY EMPIRE, ETC.

It is the opinion of the most learned that the most ancient sages, whom in Greek speech we call philosophers, if they had discovered any secrets either of nature or of art, concealed them by various methods and figures, lest they should come to the knowledge of wicked men. The more learned among the Jews confirm that Moses also, the most famous leader of the Israelite people, in his description of the creation of heaven and earth covered the secrets of ineffable mysteries with simple words. Saint Jerome too, one of the most learned among our own, affirms that almost as many mysteries lie hidden in the Apocalypse of John as there are words. I pass over the Greek sages, held in no small esteem among their own people, and our own most learned philosophers and poets, who, applying themselves to the writing of fables, by the ingenious invention of a single continuous narrative conveyed one thing to the unlearned and another to learned men. Although I cannot perfectly imitate these most devoted lovers of wisdom because of the slowness of my intellect, still I do not neglect to admire them and to read them with whatever diligence I can. For when I consider that they, by their own study, devised many things beyond other men,

PREFACE. I rub myself by a certain force, as it were, so that I may grow warm, and I drive myself toward some imitation, however slight, even with the last of those who have gone before. Nor, as I think, has this opinion wholly deceived me, since by the continual study of reading I have both learned many things that I had not known before, and by my own reflections have opened for myself, more than for others, an approach to investigating more secret and deeper mysteries.

For although my learning or industry is not so great that I would dare to profess that I have grasped in every respect that ancient method of concealing the mysteries of the sages, nevertheless I have found certain various methods, not wholly contemptible, as it seems to me, by which I can safely and without deception, suspicion, or detection by anyone disclose the most secret intention of my mind, as widely as I wish, to another who knows this art, through open messengers or open letters. And this most secret art, a new invention, at the request of the most serene prince, Lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, and ever unconquered Prince Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, the wisest of all philosophers and my Maecenas, than whom no one seemed to me more worthy for this great secret to be revealed to him, I have committed to writing and, not without very great labors, gathered into the present volume.

But lest this great secret come to the ears of common, unlearned, or wicked men, I considered it no small part of my duty, since it teaches mysteries, to wrap it in mysteries unintelligible to one who does not know how to understand, so that there will be no one from the number of the unlearned, no one unless most devoted to study, who can perfectly and fully penetrate the secret of this science by its power and according to our intention, except by receiving it from a teacher, which the Hebrews call Kabbalah, set forth in most hidden mysteries. Nor would the knowledge of this most secret art, made known among the wicked and reprobate, harm the commonwealth less than it would benefit the good. For just as good men and lovers of virtues use all aids for good and for the common utility, so evil and reprobate men seek out occasions for themselves, from evil things and also from good and most holy institutions, by which they may become worse. The same may happen to this most secret aid of ours, otherwise useful to the commonwealth and most honorable: just as it offers itself to good and most holy men as an instrument for the best purposes, so, perversely,

it offers its service to perverse and impious men for wicked deeds. For just as a good and honorable lover can, for private or common good, at any time and as often as he wishes, safely, secretly, and without any suspicion on the part of any mortal, perfectly, fully, and most completely make known the secret of his will to another who knows this art, by letters passing through everyone’s hands, whether open or closed, so that no one, however learned or curious, can suspect anything about the sender’s secret, nor, even if he does suspect it, detect it, and can disclose and express it at any distance of places; so too any perverse, wanton, or malicious man, even if previously wholly ignorant of the Latin tongue, as soon as he has acquired this art, which, with me as teacher, you will be able to acquire in two days at the longest, will thereafter write letters in Latin, with fitting composition, open in any narrative, elegant and sufficiently adorned, to me or to another skilled in this art. In these letters he will wrap the secret of his will, accessible to me alone, in such mysteries by cabalistic power that it cannot in any way be penetrated by anyone, however studious or experienced, without the spirits of this art, about which I am going to speak.

Thereafter the learned and the unlearned, man and woman, boy and old man, good and bad, chaste and wanton, in Latin or in any language known to him, would write throughout every region of the world Latin, Greek, or barbarian letters free from all suspicion, in which they would present one thing openly to those who do not know the art, and another thing secretly to those who do know it. Nor, once this knowledge had been made public among the reprobate, would the faith contracted by sacrament between married persons thereafter remain so great: for a wife, though hitherto ignorant of the Latin tongue, now sufficiently taught through chaste, honorable, and most holy words of any language or idiom, could understand most fully the evil and impure mind and intention of an adulterous or fornicating lover, even while her husband carried the letters and praised them as excellent; and in the same way, as broadly and fully as she wished, she could most safely answer her desire to him in the same or other letters, in a beautiful and quite highly adorned sequence.

Indeed, although this knowledge is in itself excellent and quite useful to the commonwealth, nevertheless, if it came to the knowledge of the depraved, which God forbid, the order of the whole commonwealth could in the course of time be disturbed in no small degree; public trust would be endangered, all letters, instruments, agreements, and finally the very [unclear] of men

PREFACE.

can be hidden, and before Jesus Christ his Son, who will judge the living and the dead, in truth I say, swear, and protest: all and each of the things that I have said in this work, or am going to say, and all the properties, modes, figures, operations, traditions, receptions, formations, inventions, institutions, mutations, alterations of this science or art, and everything that pertains to its speculation, invention, attainment, operation, and practice, either in part or in whole, and everything contained in this volume of ours, rest upon true Catholic and natural principles; and all and each are done with God, with a good conscience, without injury to the Christian faith, with the integrity of ecclesiastical tradition, without any superstition whatsoever, without idolatry, without any pact with malign spirits, explicit or implicit; without suffumigation, adoration, veneration, worship, sacrifice, or offering to demons; and without any fault or sin, venial or mortal. And all and each are done with truth, rectitude, sincerity, and purity, so that the knowledge of this invention, and its practice for good use, may not be unworthy of a wise man, a good and faithful Christian.

For I too am a Christian, voluntarily devoted to the monastic life; and I desire to live and conduct myself no otherwise than truly befits a Christian and a monk professed under the rule of the divine father Benedict. I received the Catholic faith itself from the cradle according to the tradition of the Holy Roman Church, having been baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. This faith, together with that same universal Church of Christians, I hold and believe; and as long as I live, with God’s help, always firmly preserving it inviolate, I will hold it in heart, mouth, and deed, nor do I ever intend to depart from it on any occasion whatsoever. Far be it from me, therefore, either to learn or to teach anything that is contrary to the Christian faith and its purity, harmful to holy morals, or in any way opposed to the regular life I have undertaken. I fear God, and I have sworn myself to his worship; from him I shall be separated neither living nor, as I trust, dead. This

PREFACE.

This protestation of mine I have not set before the whole of this work of ours without cause, because I know that there will be many who, when they cannot understand the things we have written, will turn to abuse, and will attribute our good and holy studies to evil arts or superstitious inventions. To these, since they will exist, and to all whoever will read this synthesis of ours, we earnestly beg that, if they understand this secret tradition of ours, they keep it forever hidden, and not pour forth such wondrous mysteries into public view. But if they do not understand it, as we know will happen to many, let them learn before they criticize. For he shows himself a rash judge who gives sentence on a matter before he has learned the truth.

Learn this art first, and afterwards judge it. If you have been unable to understand it, do not reject the art itself, since it is good, but your own dull wits. For I know and am certain that no one of sound mind can criticize this work of ours unless he happens to be wholly ignorant of it. As for those to whom it is more familiar to despise wisdom than to have learned it, I neither hope nor would wish them to penetrate these mystical matters of ours.

CHAP.

I

CHAPTER I.

WHOSE KEY AND OPERATION IS HELD by the principal spirit Pamersyel, Anoyr Madriel, through the ministry of Ebrasothean, Abrulges i Trasbiel. And Nadres Ormennitules Rablion Hamorphiel. To these let the commission of all things be made, with an exorcism.

The operation of this first chapter is very difficult and full of dangers, because of the pride and rebellion of its spirits, who obey no one unless he is highly experienced in this art. For they not only refuse to obey novices and those less tested in the art, but, if they are pressed too hard, they often injure them and afflict them with various illusions. They are malicious and faithless above all aerial spirits, and they obey absolutely no one unless compelled by the greatest sacraments; and the secret entrusted to them they often faithlessly show to others. For as soon as they have been sent out with letters, they fly away, and, bursting in disorderly fashion toward the person to whom they are sent, like a people fleeing battle without a leader, they hurry furiously and, filling the air with their shouting, often reveal the sender’s secrets to everyone in the vicinity.

We therefore advise that no one intending to work in this art compel them, nor anxiously seek their services. For they are insolent and faithless, when he can find many among those whom we shall mention below who are quite well disposed, and who of their own accord offer themselves ready for obedience. But if anyone should absolutely wish to test their insolence and prove that what we have said is true, let him know that the following procedure must be observed. Let him prepare the paper on which he is going to write with an invocation of the divine name, in the name of the Father

STEGANOGRAPHY

and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Then let him write on it whatever simple and open narrative he wishes, which all who read it may understand, in Latin, in his native language, or in any other language. But when he has sat down to write, facing the East, let him compel the spirits in this way:

Pamerfiel oshurmy delmuson Thaftoyn peano charustea melany. lyaminto colchan, paroys, madyn, moerlay, bulre atloor don melcoue peloin, ibutsyl meon mysbreath alini driaco person. Crisolnay, lemon asosle mydar, icoriel pean thalmon, asophiel il notreon banyel ocrimos esteuor naelma besro. nathaomor fronian beldodrayn bon otalmesgo mero fas el-nathyn bosramoth.

When he has said these things, and the spirits seem to him to be present to obey, let him continue the work he has begun. But if they have not yet appeared, let him repeat the words just given as often as necessary until they appear, or else let him entirely desist, lest, when compelled too much, they injure the operator. But when you have completed the letters you intend, send them by messenger to a friend tested in the art. When he has received them, let him say this conjuration:

Lamarton anoyr bulon madriel traschon ebrasothea panthenon nabrulges Camery itras-bier rubanthy nadres Calmosi ormenulan, ytules demyrabion hamorphyn.

When these words have been said, he will at once understand your mind perfectly, since the spirits will now of their own accord offer themselves with force and with shouting, so that very often other people present are able to perceive the sender’s secret. But observe that in all letters that you send written by this art you affix your own sign, so that the person to whom you write may know through which spirits you have operated. For if he himself were to operate through some spirits for understanding, but through others for sending, they would never in eternity obey him; rather, because of the improper operation, they would injure him and would by no means reveal your secret. For all the spirits whom we use in this art guard only the orders and offices entrusted to them, and in no way meddle with others. Consider carefully everything we have said in this chapter; you will be able more easily to understand what we are going to say in the following chapters. And so that

THE SECOND BOOK.

And so that we may prove by example the things we have said, let us set out our intention in the vernacular language, which we shall then make known to a friend in the manner stated before.

LET THIS BE THE SECRET INTENTION OF THE MIND of some prince, which he desires his absent vassal to know.

Roth.

Dear faithful one, we intend, for proper cause, to make war on those of Strasbourg and to fall upon them with our whole force on the next Wednesday after Vitus and Modestus. Therefore it is our earnest desire of you, since you are bound to us by oath and pledge and obligated to faithful service, that on that same day, well equipped according to your ability, you appear at four after midday near Strauffenburg in the forest. (Here the letters were placed thus.) You will find further instruction there; comply with it and do not fail to appear. We will acknowledge this graciously toward you, and keep this plan of ours with you in high secrecy, etc.

FOR MAKING THIS SECRET KNOWN

To the vassal, with the sender’s fuller intention, let it be written thus, or in another manner:

Roth.

Almighty, everlasting God, who created all things out of nothing, have mercy on us through the most bitter passion of your only-begotten Son as he died on the cross; he was conceived of the Holy Spirit without male intercourse and born of the most pure ever-Virgin Mary, and, handing himself over voluntarily to death for us, by his most holy blood, as he died, freed our souls from death. Hear us wretches, O most merciful Father, and through the outpouring of the most sacred blood of the same your sweetest Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, forgive us our sins and pour your grace into our hearts, so that, loving you in all things and above all things with sincere fervor, we may always obey your commandments with devotion and, continually advancing in mutual love, henceforth love nothing earthly and seek nothing perishable. For you are the Lord our God, who from the beginning created us in your image and likeness when we did not exist; and through your beloved

son redeemed us when we had perished; him, dead and buried for our sins, you raised from the dead on the third day, and showed him alive to his rejoicing disciples for forty days, to their great consolation. We believe, with pure and most firm confession, that he, true God and man, reigns with you in your uncircumscribable majesty without end, and that at the end of the world he will come again to judge the living and the dead, and will render to each one of us according to his works. Through him we ask you, O most merciful Father: hear us and have mercy on us now and in that terrible hour in which we are to be judged by your Son. Look upon us, most merciful God, for we are frail and pitiable sinners, bare of good works, who by sinning have offended your most holy Majesty in many things. But, turned by your mercy to penitence and humbly pleading for our sins, we ask that you turn your indignation away from us, and mercifully forgive us the crimes of the past, leading us, when this present exile is ended, to the delight of the heavenly homeland. Johannes Trithemius wrote this.

A simple and open narrative of this kind, or any other you wish, which everyone may read and understand and which contains no secret, which we have said is suitable for public view, you should write on the aforesaid paper. When the one whom you wish to know the secret intention has read the words, facing toward the East, let him turn his face to the East and say the conjuration which we set out above: Lamarton, anoyr; and at once he will certainly understand your secret intention, which you entrusted to the spirits.

TO

BOOK ONE.

FOR KNOWING THE PLACES OF THE SPIRITS, Roth., their names and signs; note what is set below.

But since it is necessary for everyone working in this science to know the places and names of the principal spirits and their signs, lest through ignorance he summon from the North one who dwells in the South, which would not only impede the intended result but could also harm the operator, I shall next set before you, in a circle, the quarters in which the principal spirits dwell, together with their names and signs.

Again, you must know the first deputies of each of the principal spirits: how many they are in number, to whom the secret mysteries are entrusted,

Here I wish you to understand by East not the place where the Sun rises on any given day, but the place in which it was created at the beginning, which we call the equinoctial place. For unless you observe this consideration most diligently, you will not be able to make progress in this art. But now I shall also teach you the sequence of that table, so that from one spirit you may understand all. Therefore let us take Malgaras as an example, through whom the operation of this art is performed in the ninth chapter of the present first book. He is western; his sign is thus: ☒ ☓. He has beneath him thirty who preside over the day and have authority to put to flight the spirits of darkness. Subject to these are another thirty, who preside over the night and always dwell in darkness, nor do they come to the light except by command of their princes, to whom they are subject at all times. And these in turn have under themselves, as it were,

BOOK ONE.

guardians and ministers, subject to them by full right, sometimes thirty, sometimes twenty, sometimes ten, and sometimes all; they go out all together, with all of them, at the command of their princes, in the following order: namely, as many of them as have been summoned by the operator, by the authority of the great Virtues, from the second or third order, so many servants and guardians also come with them to the principal spirit, who is Malgaras. Again, beneath these are others, as messengers and gatekeepers, without fixed number, who often assemble mingled with them. We do not possess the names of all these spirits. But those which it is necessary for the operator to know we shall set out in each chapter. And note that all these spirits, each with his principal emperor, are in the quarter of the world assigned to him, as is clear in the table.

CHAP. II.

WHOSE PRINCE IS CALLED PADIEL, Roth.

Subsolanus, having under himself 10,000 ministers of the day, 200,000 of the night, and many other subservient ones, whose number is uncertain.

As we said in the preceding chapter, since Pamerfiel with his spirits named there is implacable and faithless, and does not readily obey all who desire to work in this art, but scarcely even the most experienced in it, in this present chapter we wish to make the art safer and to demonstrate a method of working in it through better spirits, who are benevolent, ready, and cheerful in obeying the one who calls them, and who, when called in the proper manner and at the proper time, come without delay and faithfully carry out whatever has been entrusted to them, without any deceit. Now the first principal emperor and presiding spirit of this operation is called Padiel, by name Subsolanus, of the circular mansion, which is the first mansion after the east. He has beneath himself ten thousand who preside over the day and over all daytime operations of this art; they command and bring forth the nocturnal spirits lurking in darkness, who are two hundred thousand in number. They all flee the light and the day,

8 STEGANOGRAPHY

and day, except one who is the messenger to the presiding Spirits. All are good and well-disposed, and they do not harm the operator unless he is malicious or less skilled in the art. It is not necessary to summon all of them at once; a few suffice, and sometimes one can satisfy the operator, whether the operation is nocturnal or diurnal. For since they are well-disposed, quiet, and peaceful, they are more often solitary wanderers than tumultuous in a crowd. Therefore, when you wish to work through them and to communicate the secret of your mind through them to someone, however absent he may be, do this. Write on paper previously prepared in the proper manner, as you know, whatever narrative you wish and in whatever language, because it makes no difference, since he will perceive your mind not from the paper but from the Spirits. While writing, you shall turn yourself toward the subsolanus; when it is completed, say this conjuration:

Padiel aporsy mesarpon omeuas peludyn malpreaxo. Condusen, vlearo thersephi bayl merphon, paroys gebuly mailthomyon iltheartamarson acrimy lon peatha Casmy Chertiel, medony reabdo, lafontriaciel mal arti bulomeon abry pathulmon theoma pathormyn.

When you have completed these words, you will see two, or at least one, of the Spirits present most peacefully and ready to obey your will. To him you shall entrust your secret, and he will faithfully convey what you have commanded. But when the letters have come by messenger to the person to whom they are sent, if he is alone, well; if he is with others, let him withdraw apart if he can, or if he cannot, let him turn toward the subsolanus and say this conjuration in silence:

Padiel ariel vanerhon chio tarson phymatto merphon ampriscoledabarym, elfopihroy mesarpon amcorsy, paneryn atle pachungel thearan vtrul vt solubito beslontylas gomadyrn triamy mesarnothy.

When these words have been duly spoken, the Spirit sent will immediately appear, revealing to him perfectly, with no one else perceiving it, whatever you entrusted to be revealed to him, without deceit and without any danger. No one malicious and wicked will easily be able to work in this art; but the better and purer someone has been, the more willingly and with greater cheerfulness the Spirits obey him. And the more each person has kept this science hidden, the more easily he will operate. And note that this Padiel with his Spirits is appointed to announce secret notices for the correction, imprisonment, and punishment of wrongdoers, as we have shown in the example set below.

THE SECRET OF THE INTENTION, Roth; WHICH IS TO BE ENTRUSTED NOT TO LETTERS BUT TO THE SPIRITS OF THE SECOND DWELLING.

Someone has been denounced before a prince, and some crime of lese-majesty or any other offense is laid against him. The prince wishes him to be punished by his official, from whom he is far distant, but he does not wish to write this very thing to him, lest, if the letters are disclosed by any chance, the accused be warned and flee, or resist with the forces of friends joined to him, or attempt something sinister against the prince or the laws of the country. He writes this or any other narrative to his prefect, one which he would not fear to be read by everyone; but he entrusts the secret to the Spirit in the manner we have described above, who will faithfully tell his secret to the person to whom it is sent, provided that person has first been instructed in this art.

Sincere charity. I send you a prayer, composed rather beautifully and briefly for the devotion of penitents, which, in the fullness of my goodwill, I did not wish you alone to possess, and it is as follows. Free us, Jesus Christ, eternal savior of all good people, and forgive the offenses of the guilty; hear our groans, assuaging the storms of vices, and, renewing the oldness of conscience, lead us back to eternal paradise. Good Jesus, remit our sins to us who pray, since we have gravely offended and have often relapsed. Sweetest savior, heal our infirmities, we beseech you. Be kind to those who ask you, most pious Jesus, and hear us, your servants, as we supplicate. We are human beings, wrapped in constant miseries and plunged in the greatest storms. Deliver us, most victorious comforter of the afflicted, since our life, constantly buried in felicity, is corrupted. Have mercy at least, most merciful Jesus and savior; look upon the humility of those who love you, and do not allow us exiles to be submerged in the flood and foulness of vices, in the love of the world. Until now we have lain sluggish, and, bound by vices, we have slighted our salvation.

...we have esteemed our salvation little, and have scarcely remembered the examination to come. Most kindly Creator, be propitious to your servants, and save those weeping ones whom the most wretched vanity of the world has deceived. Alas, we have all neglected the way of Truth; but deliver us, fixed in the mud and exiles, for you are our Savior, Jesus, who despise no one. You are the unfailing joy and everlasting happiness of the saints, our hope, the glory of Christians, the light of angels, the rewarder of unconquered martyrs, the crown of virgins, the honor of widows. Good Jesus, hear us humble ones crying to you; deliver us from the present exile, granting us grace, that we may live without end. Give life, we ask, to us, your wretched servant-exiles, whom you have redeemed, that we may attain the true zeal of justice. Preserve us, almighty God, infinite majesty, boundless mercy, eternal salvation of noble souls. Amen. End of the prayer of Johannes Trithemius, abbot.

Another Prayer, Whose Conjuration Is: Padiel melion, parme, camiel busayr, ilnoma, venoga, pamelochyn.

Z Z ♦

Receive also this not unbecoming prayer. The lover of human salvation, the greatest creator of all things, imposed on us obedience to the commandments, which we are all bound to obey out of love; and to those who obey he promised the reward of possessing the tabernacle of eternal happiness. Let us look upon the obedience of Christ, which we should take care to imitate, so that we may deserve to enter into the eternal happiness promised to us, and to be joined to the everlasting mansions of the angels. Let us do penance while we can, spending precious time fruitfully. Let us beware lest death snatch us unprepared, since it refuses to grant delay to anyone. Therefore, brothers, do not delay doing penance. For death will come swiftly to you, and none of you can long escape it. Therefore behold your days passing by, beginning penance while you have time. The hour of departing from here is approaching. O death, most terrible of terrible things, how swiftly you consume us wretches, and make our very brief sojourn, full of many injuries, cruel for the miserable. Let us wake up, wretches, with Jesus our most pious Savior exhorting and bearing witness to us, so that we may accuse our shameful negligences, and with good works...

...carefully keep the ways of justice. Kindly redeemer of the human race, hear us, and grant us forgiveness of sins. O Father of mercy, be propitious to us in all our adversities. Heal, Lord, our infirm souls, since we are yours; grant to us afflicted little worms the rest of everlasting pleasantness, so that, always beholding you, we may praise you. Amen. Johannes Trithemius of Sponheim issued this, 1500.

Chapter III.

Whose prince is Camuel, having under him the spirits presiding over daytime operations, 10, and likewise over nighttime operations, 10, with the same number of sub-observers; their office is to announce the sender's arrival, way, and journey. Roth.

The first and highest of all the spirits of the third mansion toward the southeast is called Camuel. He is very benevolent and ready to send his substitutes to the person who operates in this science according to what is required. He has few ministers, to be sure, but all are good, willing, and faithful: namely ten who preside over the day, and the same number who preside over the night. They are always sent two by two to the operator from each order, since those who preside over the day do not flee darkness, nor do those who preside over the night flee light. Wherever necessity demands it, in every commission of the operator, one is assisted by the other; and when they appear visibly, then one is customarily seen standing by in a beautiful garment of mixed color, and the other in the form of a shining splendor. Often, however, they appear by effect alone, perceptible indeed, but they are not seen except when it has so pleased the operator. This Camuel, with his ministers and sub-observers, has the authority and power of announcing to an absent friend the state, will, condition, way, journeys, arrival, and departure of the sender, whenever the person who operates in this art wishes. Therefore, when you wish and operate according to your will through the angels of this mansion, you must first know who are the ten angels of Camuel who preside...

12 OF STEGANOGRAPHY preside over the day, and how many substitutes each one of them has, and likewise concerning the nocturnal ones. To know this perfectly, you will consider the present table.

Schw. Roth. S. R. R. R. X. R. R.

Rather, it seemed it should be read Noctar.

Orpeniel 10. Citgara 100. Daniel 10. Dobiel 100. Azimo 10. Camuel 100. Pariel 10. Omyel 10. Nodar 10. Tediel 0. Budiel 10. Cariel 10. Asiniel 100. Phaniel 10. Moriel 0. Elcar 10. Neriel 10. Calym 100. Meras 100. Tugaros 0.

Here in the table you have the ten angels of Camuel who preside over the day, with their substitutes in number, and as many who preside over the night, also with their own sub-servitors. The last, however, as you see, have no substitute, since 0, as you know, signifies absolutely nothing in number. Therefore, when you wish to operate through these angels, prepare your paper, as is customary; and, turned toward Eurus, write any narrative whatever, in whatever language you wish, which need not be hidden. When it is completed, read the following conjuration silently: Camuel aperoys, melym meuomanial, casmoyn eralki bufaco aeliumar photyfion theor besamys, aneal Cabelonyr thiamo vesonthy. When this conjuration has been completed in silence, make your commission to the spirits who are present, as you know; and send them forth, doing everything in silence and without disturbance, if possible. Afterwards give the letters, open as you wish, to whatever messenger you want to carry them, and let him go, because the spirits will not neglect their office, whether the messenger comes quickly or slowly. Of this let there be no doubt for you, since they are faithful. But you must know which spirit you wish to send from the aforesaid, so that in the conjuration you may express his name immediately after the principal one; and this is so in all operations in which the names of the angels to be sent are set down in the chapter itself. But now let us set forth an example of what we have said concerning those matters which pertain to the office of Camuel and of his subject spirits.

BOOK FIRST.

LET THIS BE THE MOST SECRET INTENTION OF MY MIND, which I wish to make known to someone absent through the aforesaid spirits.

[unclear] Roth. [unclear]

Suppose I am stationed at Rome, and I learn from the most secret council of the supreme pontiff that he himself wishes to transfer the Roman Empire to the Franks. I desire to notify the princes of Germany. I cannot do so by messengers, because I do not trust them; I cannot do so by letters, because in all the cities of Italy there are appointed men at the gates who inspect those passing through with the greatest care. Therefore I write one devout prayer, which I send open by a messenger, together with other closed familiar letters to those same princes. I summon the spirits of the third mansion and command them to follow the letters to be sent. And when they have been called by the recipient, they must not fail to reveal to him my secret intention, which I did not dare commit to letters. They come, they go, they obey.

We all die, because we have all contracted the hereditary guilt of original sin; and no one lives who will not die in a very short time. We contracted original fault in Adam and Eve. Moreover, all human beings die the death of the body because of the lamentable rashness of Mother Eve. But Jesus, the victor over death, drove away the death of the soul by freeing us. O crucified Jesus Christ, look upon our lowliness, for we are most wretched, unhappy, and afflicted by many tribulations. Therefore, most merciful King of the heavens, we ask: grant us contrition and forgiveness of all sins, because of your extraordinary humility by which you redeemed us from the sorrowful darkness of hell and from harmful sufferings. O our blessedness, most merciful Jesus, O sweetest lover of innocence, what shall I repay to you? You, holy and innocent, suffer for us. Where shall we flee when you come for the examination of our account? You will come with power to render reward to each person according to his conscience. And all things will be bare before you; nor will anything be hidden from you of which you do not have knowledge. Therefore, brothers, while you live, do penance, and forestall the strict examination of almighty God with works of mercy. Wipe away your crimes with tears, and by relieving the hardships of the poor, make God favorable to you. For he is kind to those who call upon him. Therefore, while there is time, seek his mercy. Always give thanks to him who redeemed you: Jesus Christ, crucified for the salvation of human beings who fear the Lord.

STEGANOGRAPHY

Roth.

LET THIS BE ANOTHER FORM OF SECRETS, WHICH IS ENTRUSTED TO THE SPIRITS.

A secret remains stored in my mind, concerning my coming soon in secret to a male friend or female friend. I do not dare write this very thing, lest it become public, which a weighty cause forbids; nor do I dare entrust it through a messenger, since there is the same danger. I summon a spirit, entrust the matter to it; it comes, goes, and carries the secret most secretly. I myself am safe in the form of the letters that I send; let it be as familiar as one likes, so that no occasion may be lacking.

Greetings in the Lord. The bearer of the present letter, brother Arnoldus Bostius, has composed many admirable volumes on various subjects, as, among many other things, you will find written at the end, where mention is made of the living, in our book sent to you some time ago, which is entitled On Ecclesiastical Writers. I commend so great a man, notable for religion and for the grace of the arts, to your sincerity, dearest patron, and I ask most earnestly that you receive him with that familiarity with which you have been accustomed to receive all those joined to us in friendship. He will disclose to you many secrets of nature, and, if you wish, will be able to delight you with the sweetest conversation. As for the codex on magical experiments which you have from me, I ask that you take care to send it back to me as quickly as possible. I shall soon send you the volume of Synesius on the power of spirits, when you have sent my experiments back to me. Take care of yourself, so that you may be well. And write back to me often. Given at Spanheim, on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1501. Johannes Trithemius, abbot.

But the recipient of the letter, the one to whom you sent the spirit, should do what he knows must be done in this art; and, once the circular sign has been recognized, let him turn toward Eurus, and in silence say this imprecation:

Camuel Busarcha, menaton enatiel, meran sayr abatremon, naculi pesum nadru lasmon enotichamabet vsear lesponty a brulmy pen sayr thubarym, gonayr asmon friachar ynon otry hamerson, buccurmy pedauellon.

When these words have been said, let him take the letters again into his hand, looking toward Eurus, as you know. But it must be noted that all these spirits, together with their prince, are toward Eurus, and therefore everyone who works through them must turn himself in that direction; or, if he cannot, at least when he has received the letters he should set them down facing that direction. Observe and understand what we have said to you.

CHAP.

[unclear]

These sixteen princes, however, with their subjects, are sufficient to announce everything to you, and you do not need either to know or to summon more. When you wish to work in Steganography through Aseliel, after the customary preliminaries in the art, observe the place of his mansion, which is in the east-south, and summon one of the spirits named above according to his time, whichever you wish. This is the conjuration:

Afelic aproysy, melyn, thulnear casinoyn, mauear burson, charny demorphanon, Theomaasmeryn diuel, casponi vearly basanys, crnoti chaua lorson.

When the conjurations have been completed in the customary way, add the remaining things that are customarily to be done in the art, and the effect of your operation will follow most certainly. Let us set down an example.

Let us imagine the secret of your mind. You have a beloved woman, in whose love you are held, and she no less; but you cannot approach or speak to her because of the watch kept by her people. At last you have found a plan by which you may possess her, but it is necessary to inform her beforehand. You cannot do it yourself; you do not dare by letters, lest they come into the hands of others; you do not judge that the matter should be entrusted to messengers or old women, lest afterward they make you known. Therefore hide by the art, for a time, a matter which you are confident cannot be done openly. You summon the invisible ministers of the art, write letters that are in no way suspicious, and send them to your beloved even through the guards themselves. They praise the writing and give it to the beloved woman to read. Recognizing the sign, she calls the hidden messenger, hears the plan, sends back her consent; you approach, enter, and possess her.

The death of Jesus Christ gave life to the human race; his life, afflicted innocently, freed us from every calamity. Therefore let us honor his humility in ourselves by resisting the temptations of vices, and by pressing on in all good works. Christ Jesus has saved our souls. Let us give eternal thanks to our most pious redeemer, since he has brought all back to safe spoils. Let us praise his name with fervor at all times, anticipating the face of his most holy majesty with our prayers. Let us live virtuously in the love of righteousness, casting off the tumult of worldly affairs; let us follow the standard of justice, resist harmful vices most devoutly, and wash away our negligences with tears

in the greatest solicitude, mindful of the future judgment, whose inestimable horror is in no way less than the punishments of hell. In the year of the Lord’s nativity 1506, on the ides of March.

When the person to whom they are sent has received these or similar letters, being skilled in the art, let him do what he knows must be done according to the instructions given in it, and let him turn himself toward the aspect of the east-south. This is its sign: ? And let him read the attestation of the spirits, which is as follows:

Asiel murnea casmodym bularcha vadusyn aty belron diuel arsephonti si pa normys orleuo cadon Venoti basramyn.

When these have been attested, let him continue the operation of the art, and he will hear the sender’s secret.

CHAPTER V.

Whose supreme prince, by name Barmiel, dwells in the south, having under him ten princes who preside over the day, and twenty who preside over the night, with their servants; and they are over the announcing of secrets that pertain to the surrender of fortresses.

The prince of the fifth mansion, in the south toward midday, is called great Barmiel. He has under his dominion ten principal leaders who preside over the day with their subservants, and twenty in number who preside over nighttime operations with their servants. These are greater in number than the daytime spirits because the operation of this mansion is carried out more often by night than by day. For their office is to announce the secret surrenders of fortresses and cities, especially at night.

When you wish to work in this art through Barmiel, summon one of his princes, whichever you wish; he will come to you at once with twenty servants, because no prince of this mansion is accustomed to go about alone or with fewer. Entrust your secret not to the servants, since they are proud and malicious, but to the prince, because he is good, calm, faithful, and very benevolent. But now I shall name for you eight of the daytime princes and likewise eight of the nighttime princes, who are better and readier to obey; we need no more.

Black. Red. R. B. G. R. R. B. Sochas 20. Aclerar 20. Barbis 20. Marcaiz 0. Red. Black. B. R. R. G. B. R. Tigara 20. Barbil 20. Marquus 20. Baabab 0.

Schw. R. S. G. R. S. Chansi 20. Carpiel 20. Caniel 20. Gabir 0. Roth. Schw. S. R. S. Ri Keriel 20. Mansi 20. Acreba 20. Astib 0.

You have sixteen spirits, of whom twelve each have twenty ministers, with whom they are accustomed to appear to one who calls them. The remaining four, beneath whom 0 has been placed, which signifies nothing, have no sub-servant, but always come alone, and in their ministry are most faithful and tireless in all things whatsoever you command them. Therefore, wishing to operate through one of them, after first performing those things that must first be performed in the art, say this conjuration toward the South: Barmiel buras melo charnotel malapos veno masphian albryon, chasmia peluo morophon apluer charmya noty Mesron alraco caspiel hoalno chorben ouear aserea cralnoty carephon elcsor bumely nesitan a̾rmy tu faron. After you have completed the command, entrust the secret to the appearing spirit whom you called; send the letters, however, through whomever you wish, and of whatever kind you wish. But let us use an example.

Let Us Suppose a Secret of a King, Which Is Not To Be Entrusted To Anyone In Any Way.

Roth.

If any prince is unable by arms to obtain a city or fortification that he desires, he attempts the matter by art; he corrupts the guards with payment. They entrust the plan to no one, not even to letters, lest, if that man is detected, he fail to achieve his purpose and they lose the payment together with their life. The prince turns himself to the mansion of Barmiel; he calls the messenger-spirit; he entrusts the hidden matter. That spirit comes and carries the message; it is captured by night, no one knows how. For these things, if it pleases, let us invent letters, in no way at all fearing the reader.

By living justly one will attain happiness; for the humble alone are to be exalted, the rash alone to be condemned. If you seek happiness, hold fast to eternal justice, and you will attain the highest glory. Be a most fervent zealot for truth, and do not love falsehood, which corrupts honor and dissolves the temperance of the mind. Flee the vanity of the world, since it is very brief. Be a lover of Justice and supplant no one unjustly. Cultivate virtues; flee vices; guard freedom with justice; beware all insolence; always be humble. Love the Savior of our souls: whoever loves him will by no means die unhappily. Contemn glory that suddenly passes away; love the blessedness of the saints, which is not to be corrupted eternally,

flee carefully the snares of our ancient enemy, whom the unfailing humility of devotion will conquer. Be watchful so that you are not overcome by the ardor of the flesh; defend the paths of justice manfully, and remember that zeal for uprightness must be held with fearless perseverance. Always flee empty glory like poison; always contemplate the loveliness of the Paradise of God, which remains forever. The joys of the world quickly pass away; today a man is glad, tomorrow stripped of all things he dies. Flee the vicious zeal of bitterness; flee the swelling of pride, since one does not fail to know that the guilt of each is liable to everlasting evils. Every proud man is hateful to God; dying without ceasing, he will be tormented and will never be consoled. What, then, will the proud await except lamentation? Therefore, woe to you, you exalted ones, worthy of eternal punishment and reserved for everlasting darkness and horrors. O vanity of the vanities of the world, destroyer of the light of souls, deceiver of exiles, most pernicious unlocker of hell. Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, wrote this on the sixth day before the Ides of March, 1500.

When the recipient of the letters has recognized Barmiel, let him at once turn himself to the South, or as soon as he can. For no danger can arise from delay with regard to the obedience of the spirit, even if much time has intervened. For when they call, he is accustomed always to come, whether they call soon or late, even after many days. This is his conjuration, after first performing the things that the art requires to be done:

Barmiel any casleon archoi bulefan eris, Cafray molaer pessaro duys anale goerno mesrue greal cusere drelnoz, parle cufureti bafriel aflymaraphe naslo, carnoserneo, damerafenotis anycarpodyn.

When he has said this conjuration, as is proper, facing the South, he will hear and understand your meaning, which you entrusted not to letters but to the spirit; if he turns himself to another region, he will never understand.

Chapter VI.

Whose supreme prince, Gediel, dwelling in the South-southwest, has under him twenty by day, and as many by night, with their servants; their office is to announce those things that have dangers to be guarded against.

The great prince Gediel presides over the sixth mansion, which is in the South-southwest. He has under his dominion twenty other principal dukes by day, and as many by night, with their many servants. Their office is to announce all things that pertain to warning a friend about any impending

concerning any imminent future danger, and especially to princes for the defense of country, castles, and cities; and to announce all things that are advantageous for friends, and for those whom we favor, toward safety, and also, conversely, against enemies and adversaries of every kind. For all these things it is not necessary to summon the twenty princes, but two suffice with their servants. So that you may know them by name, I shall consequently enumerate some of them, namely eight for the day and eight for the night.

Schw. Roth. G. R. G. R. G. R. Coliel Sariel 20 Reciel 20 Aroan 20 Naras Rantiel Sadiel Circas Roth Schw. R. G. R. G. R. G. Sabas Mashel Agra Aglas 20 20 20 20 Assiba Bariel Anael Uriel

First, before we proceed to the operation, you should know that at least two spirits must always be called, together with their twenty attendants, without whom they proceed nowhere, although they do not always all appear visibly. But this need not be a concern, provided that through their invisible ministry you obtain what you intend. Therefore, when you wish to perform anything in Steganography through their ministry, turn yourself to the south-southwest, since all of them dwell there at all times with their prince Gediel; and do what you know must be done according to the proper order. This is the conjuration:

Gediel asiel modebar mopiel, casmoyn, rochamurenu proys nasaron atido casmear vearsy maludym velachain demosar otiel masdurym sodiuiel mestray seor amarlum, laueur pealo netus fabelron.

When these things have been completed, the two named princes who have been called will be present, good, kindly, and secure. You must not fear them, but confidently entrust to them whatever you wish, and they will faithfully fulfill your command. This sign will be red.

HAVE IN YOUR MIND SUCH A SECRET as you do not dare to commit to letters.

I am bound to my prince because of many benefits promised to me. I have secretly learned of his adversaries’ plan, by treachery and betrayal, to seize the castle this night. I wish to warn my prince; I cannot do so by letters, since a search of travelers is being made by enemies on the road; I cannot do so by messengers, because I know that my danger is not to be entrusted to anyone at all. I shall call a spirit, entrust the secret, and send whatever letters I wish merely for form’s sake, so that the prince may know who is to be called; and from the number of the spirit, because otherwise without letters he would not know that a spirit had been sent by me, that one goes and announces it. The prince forestalls the seizure of the castle.

LET THE FORM OF THE LETTERS BE THIS, OR Roth. another, which, when he has read it, should forbid him to go.

The highest nobility of the human race and the highest virtue is to love God purely, to seek his glory, and to adore him with rectitude of mind. For the humility of a pure heart will reign in the heavens; patience will exalt it. The mind alone of a naked man who fears and loves God will be established in true nobility. Love God, despise the world, flee the age of iniquities; love religion, brotherly charity, the bond of peace, and the unity of those who live uprightly. Christ admonishes in the Gospel that we ought not to be anxious over superfluous human cares. “Having only the necessities,” says the holy Apostle, “let us be content.”

Therefore let us have the love of God and zeal for justice, since purity of mind, simplicity of heart, disregard for earthly honor, cleansing of comeliness, and instruction in holy morals are truly solid riches. Let us be intent upon good works, lest vices overwhelm us. Let us live innocently in all uprightness, as though about to die tomorrow. Let us love God with the purest heart, carefully keeping his commandments; with humility let us mourn for our sins at all times, beseeching the most pious Savior to forgive us our vices. To defend the honor of his love and of the heart, to rebuke the vices of the wicked, to persist in prayers, to despise the glory of the world, and to devote oneself to readings are the treasures of Christians. For the vain glory of the world is soon to collapse; riches too are false, which, when we soon expire, we leave behind unwillingly. Justice alone is our happiness; in our humility consists our glorying and the possession of riches that will remain with us forever: remembrance of death, fear of judgment, and recollection of our sins.

When these letters, or any others containing no secret, [unclear]

BOOK ONE.

I have secretly learned of a plan, through treachery and betrayal, to seize the castle tonight. I wish to warn my prince; I cannot do so by letters, since a search of travelers is being carried out by the enemies on the road; I cannot do so by messengers, because I know that my danger is to be entrusted to absolutely no one. I shall call a spirit, entrust the secret to him, and send whatever letters I wish merely for form's sake, so that the prince may know who is to be called; and from the number of the spirit, since otherwise without letters he would not know that the spirit had been sent by me, he goes, announces it, and the prince forestalls and occupies the castle.

LET THE FORM OF THE LETTERS BE THIS, OR Roth. another; when he has read it, let him forbid him to go.

The highest nobility of the human race and the highest virtue is to love God purely, to seek his glory, and to adore him with uprightness of mind. For the humility of a pure heart shall reign in heaven; patience shall exalt it; only the mind of a man stripped bare, fearing and loving God, shall be established in true nobility. Love God, despise the world, flee the age of iniquities; love religion, brotherly charity, the bond of peace, and the unity of those who live rightly. Christ warns in the Gospel that we ought not to be anxious about superfluous human cares. “Having,” says the holy Apostle, “only what is necessary, let us be content.” Therefore let us have the love of God and zeal for justice, since truly solid riches are purity of soul, simplicity of heart, disregard of earthly honor, cleansing from vanity, and the formation of holy morals. Let us be intent on good works, lest vices overwhelm us; let us live innocent in every uprightness, as though we were to die tomorrow. Let us love God with a most pure heart, carefully keeping his commandments; with humility let us grieve for our sins, at all times beseeching the most loving Savior that he remit our vices and pour into us love of himself and humility of heart. Let us abandon the desires of this world and its vain and false honors, earnestly contemplating our death. To live virtuously, to love one’s neighbor, to do injury to no one, to fear God, to give alms to the elect, to feed the hungry, to defend the good, to rebuke the vices of the wicked, to persist in prayers, to despise the glory of the world, and to devote oneself to reading are the treasures of Christians. For the vain glory of the world is about to pass away suddenly; riches too are false, which, when we shortly expire, we leave unwillingly behind. Justice alone is our happiness; in our humility are our boasting and the possession of riches that will remain with us for all time: the memory of death, fear of judgment, and recollection of our sins.

When my prince has received these or any other letters containing no secret, by the sign of Gediel he knows where it is to be turned, and which spirit is to be called.

Conjuration.

Gediel aprois camorety moschoyn diuial palorfan, fermel, asparlon Crisphe Lamedon ediur cabosyn arsythamerosyn.

When these words have been said, as is proper, and when certain other things necessary in the art have been added, with the spirit revealing not the letter but the secret of my mind, he will know the hidden matter and forestall the enemy.

CHAPTER VII.

WHOSE SUPREME PRINCE IS ASIRIEL, whose dwelling is toward the southwest, having under his dominion 20 dukes who preside over the day, and as many who preside over the night; their office is to announce the plans of princes to their friends.

The first and supreme prince of the seventh mansion is called Asiriel, and he dwells in that region of the world which we call toward the southwest, having under him 20 princes who preside over the day, and as many who preside over the night; all of them have many servants under them. If two dukes from the diurnal ones are called by the operator to the ministry of the art, they always have 10 servants serving them; similarly it is so with the nocturnal ones. Therefore, if you call only one from the princes, especially the nocturnal ones, he is proved to have not 20 but only 10 servants. You shall not call the diurnal ones unless at least two, because they are not accustomed to come alone; from the nocturnal ones you will be able to summon one or two, as you please. If you call two, you should know that 20 servants are to be added in the conjuration according to custom; if one, 10. And so that you may know who are to be called alone and who with a companion, consider the table.

Roth S. R. S. X. G.

34 OF THE STEGANOGRAPHIA

Jesus Christ, unfailing light, eternal blessedness of all the saints, creator and ruler of the universe, have mercy on us. We, weak, groaning, and weeping, beg your mercy. Grant us the power to overcome the temptations of the devil, so that, when the present evils have been conquered, we may obtain rest. O sweetest Savior Jesus, forgive the sins of us who pray. For we are yours, most merciful Father, humble creatures: look upon us, your wretched and useless servants, since we desire to serve you with all our strength. Make us possess the fervor of your love, always adorned in us with good works. Give us true works of the virtues, observance of justice, and inseparable love of uprightness; make us truly humble and vigorous despisers of worldly things, so that, always burning with your love, we may love nothing earthly and esteem nothing temporal as pleasant to us. O teacher of humility, Jesus Christ, teach us to imitate your doctrine. We are, alas, entangled in many vices, naked of good works. Save us, Jesus Christ, lest we perish. O highest Truth, give us life, most refreshing refuge of souls: be for us a tower of strength. For you are our giver of life; you are the salvation of souls and the sweetest renewer of the mind. You are the ineffable joy of the angels and the most healthful rest of faithful souls. You are the blessedness of the saints who love you. You are the inextinguishable light of the citizens above. You, giver of life to the dead, look upon our frailty. Sweetest Jesus Christ, help us, your frail servants, so that, walking without offense along the way of truth, we may obtain eternal rest. O most loving Lord Jesus, soften the labors of our exile. And when the end of this life begins to draw near, then may you deign mercifully to come to our aid, so that before the face of your power the adversary may fall terrified, and all demons, provokers of all evils, princes of eternal death, and our most savage persecutors, may flee far away. We ask through the power of your most noble death, sweetest Jesus: do not despise us, your useless servants, on the day of our departure, whom you willed to redeem with your blood. Wash away our transgressions, so that, while the angels await us, we may deserve to enter the joys of the heavenly homeland. Amen.

I, Johannes Trithemius, abbot, wrote this on the fifth day before the Ides of March, 1500.

For this reason we send letters to the person to whom the spirit also is to be sent, because none of the princes or servants from those spirits comes unless he is summoned, neither to the sender nor to the one to whom he is to be sent.

CHAPTER VIII.

WHOSE SUPREME PRINCE, MASIEREL, DWELLS TOWARD THAT QUARTER WHICH WE CALL FAVONIUS, HAVING UNDER HIM SIXTY PRINCIPAL DUKES, WITH MANY SERVANTS OF THEIRS.

The eighth mansion is toward the West, in that place from which the wind is called Favonius; and there dwells the great prince who is called Masriel, with an infinite multitude of dukes, princes, and attendants. Of these, for this art, thirty princes have been appointed who preside over operations by day, and just as many who preside by night, with many servants. All these have been established to announce and report the secrets of human arts, of philosophy, magic, necromancy, and all wondrous and most secret operations, which are known to very few people. In these matters they are ready and very faithful, nor do they return unless they have completed everything that had been entrusted to them. They are quiet and come without noise, just as they are commanded: by themselves, with many, with few, or even without servants, at least visibly. They frighten no one except the person who, not instructed in the art, has presumed to call them by the true principles of the art, to which no one easily attains by instruction. But so that you may have ready at hand those whom you should call for the operation of the spirit:

spirit: know that not all of them are necessary for you, but only some; and therefore twelve will be sufficient for you for the actions that take place by day, and as many for those that take place by night, with their servants.

Almighty, everlasting God, most just rewarder of the good, who wished your son to become a participant in our race, so that he might redeem us most wretched ones from diabolical envy; who by kindness alone, taking on the overflowing form of our nature incorrupt from the flower of the virginal womb, when the holy archangel Gabriel announced that the Virgin would conceive by your most blessed spirit, remained a perpetual Virgin, immaculate, more excellent than men and angelic spirits. The most holy and most reverend Virgin Mary, wholly without knowledge of male companionship, gave birth to the almighty king, God and man, bearing without pain, receiving without sorrow the crying God and man, always remaining immaculate, most chaste, most innocent, higher than men by the virtue of humility, full of charity, most worthy of every praise and to be venerated by all: the most blessed and always to be praised empress of the angels, most resplendent, noble, renowned, and truly most splendid. CHAPTER IX.

WHOSE PRINCE IS CALLED MALGARAS, who dwells in the west, having under him 30 dukes for daytime operations and just as many for nighttime ones; their office is to announce the private secrets of friends.

Malgaras, the greatest prince of the west, is the inhabitant of the ninth mansion, which is in the equinoctial west. He has under him 30 dukes who preside over the day, and 30 others who preside over the night, together with their servants. The office of all these is to announce to friends the secrets and hidden matters of familiar friends. The dukes are good and most ready to obey the one who calls them, especially the daytime dukes, since they are more accustomed to converse among human beings. For the nighttime dukes, although they are good, nevertheless do not willingly converse with human beings, but avoid and detest the light exceedingly, wishing to lie hidden in darkness; and for this reason they often appear to the one who calls them through conjurations like bats. From all these we shall place twenty-four by their names in the table; twelve of them in the day, and just as many at night, are sufficient.

V. 13.

Greetings and affection, my dearest and most singular friend. The bearer of the present letter, born at Roermond, is very beneficent toward our friends, an honorable man; I ask that you receive him humanely. He will explain his need to you. Since he has always been joined to me by an old connection, I would judge it most sweet, according to my powers, to relieve him and heap benefits upon him. And would that I could

Steganographia

...I could offer consolation for his misfortunes. But since I have been drained by heavy losses, as is clearer to you than daylight, I cannot satisfy my zeal as I would wish. But you, who are a kinsman and abound in worldly goods, should show yourself generous to a friend, and, as you have been accustomed, show yourself a humane patron of the necessities of friends. Therefore I ask you to lend him two hundred florins for a fixed term, because he is placed in the greatest necessity, as he will explain to you. I trust that he will restore everything in full when the term appointed for him has come. If you do this, I shall give thanks that will never die, and I shall stand by you in weightier matters. Act so that we may prove our sincere love in actual effect. I wish you to know that what you do for him is done for me; and no less will you bind him most gratefully to yourself, believe this firmly, and when the term has elapsed he will restore everything most completely. For he has been accustomed to keep his promises inviolate and to show himself steadfast toward all men.

Moreover, since you delight to hear new reports, I should like to write something. I have trained a puppy, if that is what it is rightly called by the Greek word, flourishing with such learning, discipline, and memory of all things that to some it seems to have cast off the beast and put on the human being. It understands Greek and Latin words and knows how to beg pardon for its faults. Whatever I command, it does; and when I nod by gestures, it reveals human secrets. You would see it imbued with such discipline of manners that you would judge it more learned than many men. When ordered to open a window, it opens it; and, surpassing nature by intelligence, when forbidden it puts the food back. It carries a burden placed upon it to be shown. It loves itself as the zealous defender of me, plays excellently, and does wondrous things altogether incredible to those unaccustomed to them. Farewell. Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of St. Martin in Sponheim, wrote this on 3 Ides of March, in the year 1500.

The tenth mansion is called Chorus from the wind. In it dwells the great prince Dorothiel, who has under his power and dominion forty dukes who preside over diurnal operations, and as many who preside over nocturnal operations, together with servants and attendants almost infinite in number. Their office is to announce all secret matters that pertain to spiritual business, to ecclesiastical gifts, benefices, prelacies, dignities, and the like. In the operation of Steganography, however, there is no need to bring forward the names of all Dorothiel’s dukes; rather, a few from each order are sufficient. We shall set out the names of the rest in their place with the others. And consider the table concerning these.

And note that the operation through these is very different from the others, as we shall say at length concerning the lord. For in this mansion one must operate according to the twelve hours of the day and night, and four princes always preside over two hours, both by day and by night, so that it is not permitted for you to summon any other except from the order to which the hour belongs. Let us suppose that you have such a secret of the mind, to be entrusted to absolutely no one.

You have found a very great treasure in the coffers of the dead, or in some other place in the earth, or you know for certain that it is secretly hidden. Alone you are not able to carry it away, and yet you trust no one among those dwelling nearby. You have a faithful friend, but he is far away, to whom you desire to reveal the mystery, but you trust neither letters nor messenger, lest by some mishap you fall into public exposure and danger, and lose the profit. Therefore you call the spirit. The spirit comes; he carries the message; he calls the friend. The friend comes, helps, and takes part.

Write the letter as you wish; there should be absolutely nothing in it to fear.

I am sending you the speech which I composed at the wedding of a certain female friend of mine. God, creator of all things and redeemer of the human race, and savior of all, lest the human race perish, also established the sacrament of marriage. For we read that he joined Eve as wife to the first man and said: Increase and multiply, establishing the law by which humanity was to be preserved. Afterward God, having become incarnate, deigned to sanctify weddings by a miracle. Those who serve the established order deserve well of God; but those who undertake chaste marriage out of zeal for offspring confer still more upon human beings. Therefore you who undertake honorable marriage I have rightly praised by the example of our Savior. For he, by miracles, and I, by words, shall duly praise the established and necessary sacrament of marriage. Although I am not married, I shall nevertheless rightly praise marriage. Indeed, if marriage were removed, the whole human race would fail and collapse. For by the use of marriages the human race exists, though ruinous, weak, and corruptible; yet without marriages it would not endure. But do this: let the fruitfulness of your marriage be adorned with morals and holy conduct, and put a stumbling block before no one. First of all, love God; continually devote yourselves to works of mercy together with justice; flee impiety; cultivate righteousness; love the good; always speak praises to God; assist the poor with alms; obey God’s commandments. Do not abandon truth; honor God’s ministers in the churches; pay tithes; show hospitality to pilgrims; free the innocent; feed the hungry; obey your elders...

Love God above all; continually devote yourselves to works of mercy with justice; flee impiety; cultivate righteousness; love the good; always speak praises to God; assist the poor with alms; obey the commandments of God. Do not abandon truth; honor the ministers of God in the churches; pay tithes; lodge travelers; free the innocent; feed the hungry; obey your superiors; love your neighbors honorably, doing injury to no one at all; cultivate the Christian religion most devoutly; abhor the vain, harmful, and superstitious customs of the gentiles. Keep the evangelical teachings and live according to the commandments of God. Flee the pleasures of the flesh, and show yourselves honorable and good; do not stain the purity of mind which you carefully guard. Remember, I beseech you, what Christ our Lord cried out in the holy Gospel: Blessed are the clean of heart, that is, those who preserve purity of soul in a muddy body for God’s sake. But let cleanness of heart not be lacking in continual and most humble prayers, since prayer purifies the mind, cools those who burn, and drives far away the temptations of the devil. Hence the holy Apostle Paul teaches you to persist in diligent and devout prayers, so that you may be able to overcome harmful temptations. We join you in marriage so that your family may be propagated and established by decree of the law, not so that you should overflow with harmful pleasures. For the pleasures of the flesh kill the soul and corrupt the most noble dignity of human substance, which belongs to things to come. Therefore, mindful of these things, know that you are wayfarers, destined to return to the homeland to which you have been called. The present life is very short, and the delight of the age comes most swiftly to an end. Therefore live in marriage in such a way that after death, when you are exalted, you may come to the kingdom of heaven. Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, of the order of the divine father Benedict, published this on the day before the Ides of March, in the year of the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ 1500.

CHAPTER XII.

THE SPIRIT WHOSE SUPREME COMMANDER, Cabariel, dwells toward that quarter of the world which is called Circius from the wind, and he has seventy subordinate princes by day, and as many by night.

The great commander Cabariel inhabits the twelfth mansion of the described world, which is toward that quarter from which the wind Circius blows, together with infinite spirits. Among them, fifty are appointed for the work of steganography by day, and as many by night at all times; they command many very powerful servants. The office of these spirits is to inform friends of secrets, reveal plots, and warn an absent person of those against whom he must especially be on guard. From all these we shall name a few.

Let us suppose, as an example, a certain secret to be entrusted to absolutely no one.

Steganography

You have a faithful friend, whom you favor as yourself, but he is absent far away; and you know that, when he is about to return, ambushes are to be set for him on the road by someone more powerful, or in some other place or manner. You wish to warn him, since he knows nothing; but great danger would threaten you, the warner, if it became public. Therefore it must neither be entrusted to letters, lest they be read by someone, nor confided to any man, lest it happen to be revealed. Therefore, so that you may remain safe and your friend be warned, you call the spirit and entrust the secret: it is done.

You send familiar letters to your friend, or a devout prayer, such as may bear being seen.

I had lent you my codex on the deeds of the Lombards and Bede’s volume On Times, which I ask you to send back. For it befits a wise man, and especially a Christian, to keep everywhere the faith he has promised. To forget benefits, according to divine and our human ordinances, is held to be a very great crime. Do not incur so sinful a guilt. I sent you my volumes so that you might restore them at some time. But I gave you the Greek books freely; in consideration of them, you ought rightly to show yourself grateful to us and more faithful in conduct. Farewell, from Spanheim, on the Ides of March, in the year of the Lord 1500.

When your friend has received these letters, or any others sent by you, and has recognized the sign of Cabariel, let him turn himself toward that quarter of the world from which the Circius wind comes forth; and, after first performing the customary preliminaries, let him read this prayer in silence.

Chapter XIII.

Whose prince is called Raysiel, dwelling directly to the north, under whom there are 50 princes who preside over our daytime operations, and the same number over the nighttime ones; their office is to announce betrayals.

Book One.

The thirteenth dwelling is in the north; its spirit and supreme emperor is Raysiel, who has under his dominion 50 dukes who preside over the daytime operations, with many servants, and the same number who preside over the nighttime operations with their attendants. Their office, in those causes and betrayals that pertain to death, is to warn the operator’s friends and announce the secret. The dukes who preside over daytime operations readily obey the one who calls them, and they come cheerful, pleasant, and most ready for service; but those who preside over nighttime operations are somewhat insolent, because they greatly hate and detest the light, nor do they easily obey, especially novices less proven in the art, whom they frequently laugh at to their face, unless they are so constrained by the operator’s conjurations that they cannot prevail in resisting. For they fear the conjuration greatly, and, as though in one respect, they allow themselves to be conjured more than the daytime spirits; and yet they obey unwillingly. But now, from the number of all these, let us set down the names of a few and the number of servants, as many as are sufficient for us for the customary operation.
