I have a secret of this sort, which I trust no one to carry.

I put the case. I have a certain noble and learned friend, whom I know is to be killed secretly by certain hired assassins. I do not dare warn him openly, because it is dangerous for me. In a familiar and more secret matter, I fear that letters may come into others’ hands. I do not presume to trust a man to speak it by mouth, because he who is with me today may perhaps stand against me tomorrow. And so I flee to the customary art, in which, whatever I entrust to it, I do not fear that it will become public, even if it should happen to be attempted by an enemy.

I send familiar letters to my friend, in which I fear no danger.

The ancients define the greatest ornament of nobility as justice and philosophy, and disgrace as impiety and ignorance. For what is more beautiful than to adorn with letters and virtues a noble lineage that bears arms? We find that very many most noble men, and many others serving as soldiers, have labored at this day and night, so that they might conquer barbarians with arms and instruct their own people in uprightness and letters. Following their example, most learned Bumavy, you do not cease to unfold humane letters and the good arts, adorned with arms and letters; and once the wisest ancient princes were accustomed not to shut up their wealth in their treasuries, but rather to apply it to literary use, judging the study of wisdom to be a most honorable support for those tending toward happiness, by which the blessedness of eternal reward is acquired. Indeed, knowledge of the scriptures makes princes venerable to all and especially to be feared; ignorance of the scriptures, called the burial of a living man, is accustomed to bring shame and dreadful calamity upon princes and nobles.

BOOK ONE.

41

A man without letters is a two-footed ass, to be buried alive, indeed buried more than once. Especially nobles and those governing the commonwealth ought to be wise and notable for knowledge of letters, ignorance of which brings in tyranny. Love of letters also commends to perpetuity the illustrious deeds of princes and nobles. For we see that the ancient philosophers obtained remembrance and achieved immortality of name among all people forever more by letters than by arms. For letters, more than arms, made our ancients and princes glorious, excellent, and wise, and granted the titles of praise to their memory with immortality. Add that for Christians literary study provides the highest and most honorable help for flying up to heaven. For from the scriptures we begin to contemplate the flashing and honorable majesty of divine illuminations, otherwise inaccessible to us. Therefore, Henry, most learned knight, favor letters in such a way that, adorned with uprightness, you may always live. Farewell, from Spanheim, on the day of March, in the year 1500.

Let us set down as an example any secret whatever, to be entrusted to absolutely no one.

You have some very secret business for a friend, concerning both you and him, whose disclosure would bring either lasting harm or disgrace upon you and him. Certainly it is not safely entrusted to letters, lest they be read by someone, nor committed to a messenger, who would divulge it to many. You will use our art; thus you too will be safe, and your friend will know the secret. For this purpose let us compose whatever little letter seems suitable, in no respect at all suspicious.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, to the excellent young man Jacobus Trithemius, his dearest brother: greetings.

Devoting yourself to letters, preserve humility of heart. Good morals adorn young men and make them more distinguished than nobles. Knowledge of letters adorns a young man who loves holiness; without the morals of justice, knowledge will lack honor. A youth immersed in vanities and vices, a despiser of wisdom, does not love true wisdom, which you should remember must be sought through virtues. The instruction of youths to be educated is adorned by morals, since honor is conferred upon the heavenly arts, and unfruitful knowledge will be tortured with eternal torments. He advances in the knowledge of virtues and letters; both fail when stained by vice. Spurn pleasures, so that by experience you may understand the truth of wisdom. Farewell.

Let us form,

Of the Steganography 45

for the sake of example, such a secret as must be entrusted to no one.

I have a certain secret for my prince which must be communicated to absolutely no one. I do not dare commit it to letters, lest through negligence or forgetfulness they be scattered and read; much less do I wish to announce it through a man, lest it happen in some way to be revealed through him to others also. Therefore it pleases me to test the mystery of this art, through which my secret will remain hidden at all times.

Let us write letters, of whatever sort we please, which need fear no one’s sight.

To the Most Serene Prince, Lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, Arch-Steward of the Holy Roman Empire, Prince Elector, Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, with prayers, offers his service.

Most illustrious prince, with humble submission I offer my service. The kindness of your renowned dukedom commanded me to commit to writing certain very hidden matters which had been set forth in words. I would rejoice, not without devout exultation, if powers equal to the will were present: to distribute the most honorable benefit shown, and a more suitable place, and to offer the service owed by grace. The novelty of the work, which must be undertaken without the path of a predecessor, restrains the weakness of my heart; I know myself to be far unequal to it. For it will have an immense and great labor, and it casts a very great dullness upon my efforts. Yet I shall test my powers, in obedience to Your Grace, without doubt approaching a most kindly judge, if the possibility suited to completion has not attended my good will. There, with most abundant humanity, I perceive that a glorious and most munificent prince, lover and defender of letters, speaks; under his most humane protection the University of Heidelberg, adorned with many most learned and most erudite men, most fresh in talent, surpasses all the schools throughout Germany. And so, most renowned and most humane Prince, if I have or am anything, I know it all to be bound to your kindness; and I shall always take care to offer it with humble submission most readily. And although there are others wiser, who could render this work better or more usefully and more ornately, not in mediocre fashion

48 STEGANOGRAPHY

Since I know, dearest brother, that you are a lover of the good arts, it greatly delights me to exhort you to persevere in searching out and continually turning over the secrets of books, which show us the road to happiness and the open path back into the homeland that we lost by sinning. To that homeland the burning love of our most gentle and clement Savior, hidden for us in the holy Scriptures, will lead us back, if we adorn the mind with virtues and exercise ourselves in holy study; this will without doubt be granted. For what could be more wholesome or sweeter for those wandering in miserable exile than to devote themselves diligently to letters? Through their study our eyes are lifted up to seek truth, and our mind is raised to the desire for future blessedness. Without them, the soul, submerged in temporal and worldly affairs, is compared to beasts and will never arrive at the knowledge of God. Therefore despise the pleasures and commotions of the world, and devote yourself to letters day and night; for religion is adorned by virtues, and virtues in turn by the commerce of letters. Thus one cannot value letters without the ornament of noble virtues, nor good virtues without knowledge of the Scriptures. Therefore I exhort you always to devote yourself to the study of letters. Farewell from Spanheim, 16 Kal. Apr., in the year of the Lord M.D.

Thus, if anything to be announced should perhaps occur to someone, concerning which no commission is found in the foregoing, it may be referred to these, who in their own way have commission over all matters; yet so that the general does not derogate from the special, nor the special, if not expressed clearly enough, refuse the office of the general.

Behold, mortals, the brevity and misery of the present life, and practice saving repentance while you have time. Woe to you, most senseless lovers of worldly glory, who rashly despise almighty God and eternal gladness. Why do you not love those heavenly banquets that have been promised to those who humbly seek God? For you, having cast aside humility, seek the very brief joys of the world; you do not love the excellence of eternal blessedness. You live in contentious zeal; you stain honor with wicked actions and do not know the praises of the Most High God. Day and night you devote yourselves to worldly actions and temporal gains; always intent on hunting after novelties, you sharpen your memory, but neglect to hear readings. You do not care for the time of grace granted to you, nor for the expectation of eternal blessedness. Behold, the Judge, terrible to all criminals, approaches. Behold, the stern Almighty Majesty hastens. Behold, the Last Judgment is established. Behold, eternal lamentations are set forth; everlasting goods will be withdrawn from us.

A Secret Very Hidden and Necessary for Me to Send to a Friend.

I have a certain secret for a friend, which I do not trust to be conveyed either by a man or by letters, since if it came into public view it would create great danger and harm for me. I cannot endure delay; therefore I call a spirit, and write letters that are not at all suspicious, and which he himself is not thought even to understand, since he is ignorant of the Latin language. I send the spirit; he reveals the secret.

I Send Letters of Whatever Sort, Which an Invisible Spirit May Accompany.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to the noble and vigorous knight Alberto Goeler of Ravensburg, prefect of Kreuznach, greetings.

We believe that our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, is to come for judgment, who will render to each one according to his works. We believe this, and yet, wretched as we are, we neglect ourselves. Therefore let us strive to anticipate his face with continual tears, amending the negligences we have committed, lest that terrible coming of our Redeemer overtake us unprepared; all of us must necessarily meet him, to receive the reward of our deserts. Why, then, do we now make little of the opportune time of salvation granted to us, which the Almighty has conceded to us as so useful and so acceptable? Why do we not emulate men distinguished in morals, who seek out for us examples of justice, honorable conduct, humility, chastity, and all the virtues? Let us do penance, emulating their name, since the end of our life is near. Horrible death will come, which does not know how to spare, but will devour young men and maidens, and old men together with the young. Let us live in mourning, washing away our excesses with continual tears, lest unexpected death seize us and subject us to a horrible judgment. Let us amend our past life, praying God that after

the briefness of the present sojourn he may grant us eternal blessedness. Amen. Farewell. Given at Sponheim, 14 Kalends of April, in the year 1500.

When you have received these letters, or any others committed by me to a spirit, the friend to whom they are sent, being tested in the art, after the sign of the prince of this region has been recognized and after the preliminaries have first been performed, should say the conjuration:

Toward the North dwells the great prince Demoriel, having under his dominion 400 chief princes and dukes, whom he sends into the ministry of this art according to their orders, together with subdukes and counts, whose number is not less than 600, for announcing all secrets that we wish to send toward the North to friends skilled in this art. From all those mentioned above, let us set down only as many names as are necessary for us at present, with the number of their counts and servants according to their orders in the hours.

Suppose I have such a secret, or any other whatever, to communicate.

I have a close friend, at this time far away, to whom I have a very secret matter, which cannot safely be entrusted to anyone at all, not even to letters. Therefore, so that the secret may remain hidden, I always like to call some spirit from the art who is familiar to me. I entrust the secret: he comes, goes, acts faithfully, and carries to my friend what I have entrusted; we are both safe. He himself also brings back to me from my friend a secret reply, which he tells to no other mortal. But so that the friend himself may understand that the spirit has been sent to him, it is necessary that letters of any sort, fearing nothing, be devised, in which he may recognize the sign of the spirit sent. For the spirit does not appear unless compelled.

Let us first send whatever letters we please, such as need fear the sight of no one.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Jakob Wimpfeling of Sélestat, theologian, poet, and most eloquent orator, greetings.

I should very much like, Jakob Wimpfeling, for you at last, even if late, to satisfy your promise and my expectation of you. You know what you promised, and you are not ignorant of what I expect. I do not wish you to become a monk, but to live with monks. Hasten; let us live together. Behold, the hour of our passing is at hand, greatly to be feared. Why then do we delay? Why, unhappy men, do we neglect the brief and wretched condition of our sojourn

  1. STEGANOGRAPHIA

here? Why do we refuse, in this saving time, to do penance for the offenses of our transgressions? Let us prepare ourselves for death, since it hastens terribly enough, calls all the reprobate, spares no one, reveres no one; it denies a hearing to those who pray; it despises the tears of the [unclear]; it scorns the threats of princes and destroys their kingdoms, names, and glory; it brings to nothing the hateful pride of tyrants before all. Therefore, brother, diligently considering the benefits bestowed by the Redeemer, very useful to us, recompensed by many things, correcting what is ours, shining continually with good morals, so that by penance and tears we may be able to appease the strict examination of the judge hastening to the seat of judgment, who will show himself terrible to the [unclear] and joyful to the elect. Farewell, from Sponheim, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord 1500.

CHAPTER XXI.

Whose supreme emperor and prince is called Geradiel, dwelling in no quarter of the world, but wandering and accustomed to be present everywhere.

Besides those emperors, princes, and dukes of spirits whom we have named in the preceding chapters, who remain in fixed places throughout the visible world, there are also many others assigned: wandering, unstable, and remaining nowhere fixed. The ancient wise men and magi called these aerial, that is, unstable, because they fly in the air like flies, without order, without dwelling, and without restraint. Of these, some are not useless to us for Steganography, because they do not require the observance of places, but can be summoned by conjuration in every place. The first

FIRST BOOK.

The first of these is called Geradiel. He has no duke or prince under him, but only many and almost innumerable servants, whom he takes with him for service according to the ranks that they have among themselves, and according to the 24 hours of day and night. Their general office is to announce all secrets, whatever they may be and to whatever region you wish.

Hours of day and night.

I send letters merely for form’s sake, so that people may be deceived; and the one to whom I send them should know from the sign written below which spirit he ought to call, since they are not compelled.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, sends work to all learned and curious men reading in this art without a teacher.

Amend your life from the root. The strict examination of judgment will suddenly seize everyone, no one being safe, and in its bitterness and eternal griefs will fill the vicious; it will not dare to sadden the saints. With wailing, deplore your sins, most wretched and most foolish people. See, without good exercises you reject the name of religion. Do you not know that an examination is coming upon the guilty? The final hour approaches; we shall not live long, but all of us will be compelled horribly and unexpectedly to pass away. Therefore do not neglect the time; honor the grace granted to you by works. From Sponheim, on the 13th day before the Kalends of April, in the year 1500. X.

CHAPTER XXII.

Whose prince is Buriel, nocturnal, a fleer from light, and dwelling in lakes and in the holes of the earth; and no operation is performed through him except at night.

After Geradiel follows Buriel, indeed a great prince, but perverse and wicked, who hates, persecutes, and detests all other spirits, especially princes; but he is no less hated by them. He fears and flees the light with all his leaders and servants, nor is he ever accustomed to come except at night, and this often with great horror and fear for the operator, especially if he is not perfected in the art, steadfast, and strong in spirit. And he often appears in the form of a serpent, having a maiden’s head, but a tail and whole body like a serpent, hissing terribly. When adjured in the proper way, he speaks in human words. He has under him leaders and princes, whom he is accustomed to send into service with their attendants and servants, whose multitude is almost innumerable. From these let us set down the names of some who may suffice for our operation.

When you have spoken this verse in silence, always looking at the ground, the spirits called will be present. But take care not to be afraid, because they will not be able to harm you if you are brave and steadfast in spirit. And note that these princes or spirits, although they are generally appointed to announce all nocturnal secrets in the night, are nevertheless especially suited and willing to carry a message to prisons and lakes, to captives, and likewise in matters that pertain to carnal love and the hidden practices of lovers, and for everything that happens in the night, whether good or evil, because they hate the light.

Let us suppose a secret which is by no means to be entrusted to anyone, as follows:

I have a secret for a friend established in this city, which I can make known to him neither by letters nor by a messenger, lest it become public. Several things prevent me from going to my friend myself. I call one of the aforesaid spirits; I entrust the mystery to him; he goes and faithfully announces what I have committed to him. I am safe.

I shall compose letters of whatever sort I wish, which should make no one suspicious, namely, such as these.

Our Savior Jesus Christ, who, dying on the Cross, redeemed the human race by his blood, is to be praised by us earnestly and without interruption. He promised that he would drive away death and give eternal life to us who fear and love him. Now therefore, dearest brothers, let us rise up from our sins, preparing our lamps with good works, so that we may meet our Redeemer joyfully in the hour of the fearful passage, when death will snatch away our souls. We now have abundant time for completing penance and adorning our lamps; but at the final hour of death, further space for repentance will be wholly denied to us. Let us consider the very brief glory of the world, since it is empty: it passes most swiftly;

nor are we corrupted with it at every hour. Therefore let us humble our hearts at all times, never failing. In the year 1513, April 8.

CHAPTER XXIII.

WHOSE SPIRIT AND SUPREME PRINCE IS CALLED HYDRIEL, AND DWELLS IN THE WATERS; HE HAS UNDER HIM 100 DUKES, 200 COUNTS, AND ALMOST INNUMERABLE SERVANTS.

There is another prince among the principal spirits, who is called Hydriel, and he dwells in waters, ponds, lakes, marshes, and the sea, and around springs, cisterns, and rivers. He has under his dominion at least 100 dukes, his princes, and 200 counts, his sub-dukes, and many servants. Their office in general is to announce all things both by water and by land, whether by day or by night. And know that the princes are sufficiently benevolent and willing in all things, but when they come after being conjured, they do not appear so. For they frequently appear in the form of a serpent, sometimes large, sometimes small, having the very beautiful head of a maiden, with hair spread out. None of them goes alone, but each prince brings with him at least two counts and 80 servants. So that you may not fall into error in the operation, I shall give you the names of some of the dukes.

Chapter 24.

Whose prince is called Pyrichiel, having under him many dukes, princes, counts, and servants, whose number is uncertain.

Pyrichiel, a certain supreme prince of spirits, does not seem to us to be altogether rejected from our art, because he is said to be quite benevolent.

He does not have under him dukes or princes in the manner of the others, but only counts and subordinate servants, whose number is uncertain. There are some who say that he has dukes and princes under him; but they seem to us not to understand his property and custom sufficiently, since they have imagined counts and servants to be dukes. The name Pyrichiel derives its word from fire, because he is accustomed often to be around fire.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, to the Reverend Father and Lord Nicolaus, Bishop of Irburga, vicar of the Archbishop of Pantomora, greeting and due service.

When I call to mind your intellect and the honesty of your life, I am strongly compelled to declare you, most Reverend and excellent Father, the most worthy of all bishops. For truly, if I should speak of the innocence of your life, I would call you most just, most learned in all letters, and venerable for your most holy morals. You adorn your conduct with works of righteousness, and you always show yourself an excellent shepherd of souls; and in letters you continually exercise yourself by study, so that you may confer benefit on yourself and on others in both respects. Farewell. Given from Spanheim, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1500.

I have a friend far away, skilled in the art of Steganography, to whom I have a great secret and mystery which must not be entrusted to anyone, even by letters, nor disclosed. Therefore, so that all things may remain secret, I send as messenger a spirit who will reveal the secret to my friend and keep my business secret.

Let us amend our life, humbling ourselves before the supreme ruler of the universe. Humility gains heaven, destroys the harmful temptations of demons, breaks down the pernicious swelling of the mind, and powerfully drives out all fires of vices. The path of humility deserves to receive a crown and to possess a noble kingdom. I have set the path for you: innocence, uprightness of conduct. By guarding it continually, you will not sin. This alone is the way for us to heap up the merit of blessedness: that, giving thanks to God, we may fear him with a most upright heart, fleeing the tumult of the world; that we may never grow weary of the practice of humility, while seeking the life above. Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, wrote this on 10 Kalends of April, 1500.

Let us compose the letter at will.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Spanheim of the Order of Saint Benedict, sends greetings to the Reverend Father Lord Rutgerus Sycambro, archbishop of Narvia.

Nicolaus, the most reverend and most studious bishop of Irbursen, will explain to you that the general governor of your ecclesiastical affairs has handled the matter badly: he subjected the vicar of our lord King Desiderius, a kindly man, to chains, and killed him, tortured by hunger. We daily expect King Desiderius, the enemy, to break into the diocese. But we entreat you: come quickly to our aid, so that you may not fall into the enemy’s hands. Farewell. 9 Kalends of April, M.D. 3.

Great and eternal are the future benefits of those who preserve innocence: that men rejoicing should be present amid angelic praises; that they should behold that exalted light, the splendor of eternal blessedness, and see the face of majesty in its own proper light. Let there be a secret for a prince.

The prefect of a king or prince, appointed in a land or province, has learned by a most secret report that the enemy shortly intends to break into the province. He wishes to inform the prince, but cannot do so by messengers, because they are to be tortured by the adversaries on the way so that they may betray the secret; nor by letters, since all will be opened by them. Therefore he calls the spirit, entrusts the secret, and composes other letters.

Let us compose letters conveying nothing useful.

We ask, sweetest of friends, that, in view of our old friendship, you would quickly send us your copy of Tertullian, that most noble and most wise man, to be returned after copying,

76 Of Steganography

and also Bernard's letter to the Templars. We all know that the glorious name of Catholic sanctity was given to Tertullian of old among our people, and we know that he, a noble light of sacred faith, did not remain the least. He was outstanding in his actions, a glorious teacher of divine law, a most devoted defender of our liberty. Although he is censured in some matters, he nevertheless wrote honorable volumes in expounding our faith. He had a wife zealous for our religion and a lover of it, noble in humility and innocence, glorious in chastity. Some praiseworthy writings of his correct instruction survive, sweet and overflowing with much doctrine; brief letters, not useless, honorably and graciously exhorting us to the pursuit of eternal glory. 8 Kalends of April. In the year 1500. Johannes Trithemius wrote this.

The glory of ineffable eternal blessedness is acquired by good exercises and humble ones. Now, with diligent tears, wipe away your errors, mortals; love God,

love and adore his holy name. Learn humbly to imitate the path of humble, crucified Jesus Christ, always rendering honor to him, sweetly burning with love for our most gracious savior. In this table we have set down thirty-one principal spirits, who preside, each in his own office and order, over all the operations of our Steganography, about which we have spoken in this first book of ours. We have assigned to each the character appropriate to him, and have also added the number and order of princes, dukes, counts, servants, and subservient spirits in their proper ranks, so that no one who desires to study this art may fall into error because of the diversity of the operations.

The great mysteries of this art can be penetrated only by the most studious men: namely, those whom love of secrets and nature urge on to investigation, and who, in their desire to obtain knowledge, refuse no honest and possible labor. But as for men who are lazy and dull in intelligence, whom neither love inflames toward the study of the secrets of wisdom nor nature assists, when they have been unable to understand this most secret art of our invention, understand that this should not be imputed to us, but rather ascribed to their own sluggishness, idleness, and malice. For either, having their intellect immersed in the pleasures of the flesh and worldly cares, they cannot devote themselves diligently to examining these matters, or, already considering themselves wise or very learned, they despise our compositions as unworthy of their reading.

There will also be some who are so accustomed to stand by old traditions and those of others that whatever they have not learned in them they think either impossible or superstitious. Nothing is more unfit than these people for the knowledge of this profound art, since they either do not wish or are not able to contemplate its highest matters. But those who are both capable and willing to study this art, if any such shall exist, we have resolved to admonish briefly at the end of this book, so that they may be able to make progress.

First of all, they must be warned always to keep the art itself hidden, lest it penetrate into the hands and knowledge of the wicked, who would commit many execrable crimes through it. For although the art itself is truly good in itself, nevertheless its practice would conduce no less to evil through the impious than to good through the good. Therefore let that remain secret among the good which, if made public among the wicked, would do harm. Yet the good should not therefore despise this knowledge because it serves the wicked for evil, just as one does not despise the sword because it lays a man low.

Next, students of this art must be warned not to presume to proceed to operate in it unless they have first [unclear].

The great mysteries of this art can indeed be penetrated only by the most studious men: namely, those whom love of secrets and nature itself move to perseverance, and who, in their desire to attain knowledge, refuse no honorable and possible labor. But men who are sluggish and dull in intellect, and whom neither love kindles toward the study of the secrets of wisdom nor nature assists, when they have been unable to understand this most secret art of our invention, should understand that this is not to be imputed to us, but rather ascribed to their own dullness, laziness, and malice. For either, having their understanding immersed in the pleasures of the flesh and worldly cares, they cannot devote themselves diligently to examining these things, or, already considering themselves wise or most learned, they despise our compositions as unworthy of their reading. There will also be some so accustomed to rely on old and other men's traditions that whatever they do not find in them they judge either impossible or superstitious. Nothing is more unfit for knowledge of this profound art than such men, who either will not or cannot contemplate its highest matters.

But those who are both apt and willing to study this art, if any such there are to be, we have resolved to admonish briefly at the end of this book, so that they may be able to make progress. First, they must be admonished always to keep the art itself hidden, lest it come into the hands and knowledge of the wicked, who would commit many detestable crimes by means of it. For even if the art itself is truly good in itself, nevertheless its practice would conduce no less to evil through the impious than to good through the good. Let that therefore remain a secret among the good which, if made public among the bad, would do harm. Yet good men should not on that account despise this knowledge because it serves bad men for evil, just as one does not despise the sword because it strikes down a man.

Next, students of this art must be admonished not to presume to proceed to operate in it unless they have first been perfectly instructed in everything that is required for practical knowledge.

Book One.

For I am not unaware to what great dangers they expose the matter who, being insufficiently skilled in it, have ever attempted to perform anything.

Likewise, whoever is well instructed in this knowledge and wishes to operate through it should remember diligently to observe, according to what we have said both in the circle and in the individual tables and chapters, the distinction, places, names, orders, and offices of the supreme spirits, and also their dukes, how many counts there are in number, what order they observe, and how many they set over the substitutes, so that he may know how to express these things in the conjuration. For unless the operator of the art has carefully kept all these things, he will not be able to make progress or to reach the effect of his intention.

Again, let him attend carefully when each spirit is to be called, and for what offices or secrets to be announced, and to what region of the world he belongs, lest he err either in the places or in all the matters concerning the individuals, or any of those whom he wishes to call.

Likewise, let everyone who is advised and is about to operate in this knowledge attend most diligently to pronounce the words of the conjurations properly, in which the great force of our operation consists; for when an error is committed in the conjurations, the spirits called and to be called not only do not obey, but even resist altogether. Consequently, let him also be forewarned not to call one for another, but each one in his own order, time, and office, just as has been sufficiently stated by us in almost all the chapters of this book. For if, either from error or from any other negligence, he calls one for another, he will make no progress in his operation, but will rather bring danger upon himself.

Likewise, in the conjurations let him name the spirit who is called together with his substitutes, and let the cause of the calling be settled beforehand in the intention; nor should the act of operation be performed in trivial and profane matters, which one person could otherwise safely communicate to another without danger, either by letters or by messengers. For this art is to be used only for announcing great and difficult matters which, if made public, would bring loss or danger to the operator. Likewise, it is necessary for everyone operating in this art to know the natures of the spirits: which are good, which evil, which prompt and benevolent toward obedience, which hard and rebellious. Again, [unclear]

Book Two

85

...the services may abundantly suffice for every operator. Yet, lest we seem to omit anything that can contribute to the perfection of this art, we have resolved to join a second book to the first.

Since, according to the tradition of certain wise men, individual spirits are assigned to each hour of day and night for various operations and diverse, wondrous effects, it has pleased us to imitate only their order, not their superstition: so that we may take from it, without injury to the Christian name, what conduces to our purpose, while we pass over the rest with contempt, as full of magical arts and contrary to our faith. Therefore, taking up the principal spirits assigned to the several hours, both of day and of night, according to the secret teaching of Solomon, surnamed Hermes, in his volume On Magic, as supreme emperors of the art, together with the other officers necessary to us for the proposed operation, we shall proceed. And we shall give both method and instruction to all students of this art, by which they may at any hour, with safer counsel, make known to friends the secret and hidden conception of their minds.

For each prince presides over his spirits, dukes, counts, and servants as a watcher. At his command, when called by us with the lawful song, they come; they carry the secrets entrusted to them, and show themselves obedient to us and ready in all things. But since I am again going to make mention of spirits, I think I must once more say beforehand: nothing frivolous is contained in this our art; nothing contrary to evangelical tradition or the Catholic faith; nothing at all superstitious is taught. For all the things that we have said in the preceding volume, or shall say in the following ones, rest upon natural, lawful, and honorable principles. Only the mystery veiled by foreign usages, and the words wrapped in the names of spirits, require an educated reader. For we use the service of a spirit to veil a secret which, if made public, would harm the wicked. And lest anyone fail through error in reckoning the hours, let him know that we have taken the hours of the planets both in the day and in the night.

Chapter I

Samael, the supreme emperor of the first hour, presides over the first hour of the day. He has under his command several dukes, counts, and servants, whom he sends, when called in this hour only, to an operator experienced in Steganography.

The spirit and emperor of the first hour of the day, which takes its beginning at sunrise, is called Samael. He has under his command very many dukes, counts, and sub-servants, who, when called by an operator in Steganography, come in this hour alone. They carry the secret that is entrusted to them, but they utterly refuse to come outside the hour. And note that the dukes and first princes of Samael are rarely sent by him for the service of this science, since their office is to stir up magical and nocturnal illusions among human beings.

16 Steganographia

The counts, however, together with their servants, have been specially appointed to the ministry of this art. They are also more often sent to it without the presence of the dukes. Since they are from the highest order among spirits, they are accustomed to show themselves somewhat proud and rebellious toward those who call them, nor do they easily obey anyone, unless he is most skilled in the art of Steganography, without labor and danger. For they are insolent and very ready for illusions and mockeries of men, and they deride and jeer especially at those whom they have found to be less skilled in the art of Steganography. But those whom they judge to be bold, steadfast, and experienced in this art itself, they revere and fear, and they always obey their commands most promptly, with trembling and reverence. Therefore we shall now report the names of those of their counts who are necessary to us in operations of Steganography at this hour.

And when you have completed this, write this conjuration on the back of the same sheet in silence, saying nothing.

When this conjuration has been written on the sheet, as stated above, clearly and distinctly, you will prepare the letters to be sent to the one whom you wish to know the secret, in whatever form pleases you,

because it makes no difference in what form the letters to be sent have been composed, provided they contain no secret in themselves. Then, when the letters too have been written, call one or two of the counts according to the order, if you are working many times in this same first hour of the day, and say the conjuration prescribed from the same sheet, with the strongest intention, fearing nothing. When it has been duly completed, the spirits called will at once appear to you visibly, in a familiar form and one customary to them, calm, benevolent, and most ready for every service that arises. When they have appeared, entrust your secret to the principal one among them, saying: Ameniel, by the hidden power of this conjuration I command you to go as quickly as possible to Albertus Goelet of Ravensburg, prefect in Kreuznach, and to tell him in my name thus and thus. Having said these things, add the secret word, which must not be written; and immediately the spirit will fly away. Send the letters, sealed with the character of Samael, as is customary, by a messenger; they should contain no secret and should fear no one’s inspection.

Let the secret be whatever occurs:

Let it be a great secret, and an arduous one, whatever occurs for the occasion, and of such a kind that it ought to be communicated to no one: it must not be entrusted either to letters or to couriers. For in this art, especially through the spirits of this second volume, one must not work for small and trivial causes that can otherwise be announced by letters.

You will compose the letters concerning these matters as you please.

The majesty of the Catholic faith, to be firmly preserved by all men, has promised the happiness of eternal life to those who serve Christ. Hold the Catholic Christian faith; glorify the Almighty, fleeing the turmoil of vanity. No one of wicked deeds will have the blessed life. Let the faithful man follow Christ on the path of virtues. Integrity is adorned by good works, and the Catholic name is preserved by Christian faithfulness. For a wicked man clouds over the faith. Christ hates the rash, and loves Christians who practice Catholic works and revere tranquility. Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, published this on the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord 1500. When you have received the letters, let the one to whom they are sent first perform in the art:

let him first perform those things which, according to the general instruction of the art, must be done beforehand; and let him say the prescribed conjuration in the manner and rite that we have already described, written on a sheet with the character of the lord of the ascendant and the other things expressed. But as soon as he has completed the conjuration, he will see the spirit present. When he has seen him, let him say without fear: penador auenal † solmenial phanu † sauear caschanti hernoty maduran. Amen. The crosses are red. When these words have been said, let him be silent, and he will see the spirit approaching him and reporting the entrusted secret into his ear, secretly and securely. Let him hear him without fear and with such great diligence that, if anyone is sitting nearby, he does not indicate the spirit’s presence either by nod or by word.

THE SECOND HOUR OF THE DAY IS CALLED CEVORYM. Its prince and supreme spirit is Anael, who has under his rule 10 dukes, counts, centurions, and 100 presidents. There is no fixed number of servants and subservants.

The second hour of the day is called Cevorym, in which changeable operations are performed, amazing to all human beings. All the spirits of this emperor are sufficiently benevolent, pleasant, cheerful, and most ready to obey the operator in the art, provided that he is skilled in the art, strong in mind, constant, and understanding well.

When the conjuration has been written, do the other things which you know must be done according to the art. Then say the song in silence, and at once you will see the spirit present, cheerful, pleasant, and benevolent toward all things; to him you may securely entrust the secret.

Let us set down any secret whatever.

Let the secret be any matter that occurs at the time, which seems neither useful to commit to letters nor to be entrusted to a messenger. From the spirits of Anael let one duke and one count be summoned, or one or the other of them, as you please. Let the secret be entrusted to the more principal spirit in the proper manner, as is required according to the precept of the art, and he will carry it faithfully.

Let the tenor of the letter be familiar.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Wilhelm Veldicus, Canon of Saint Augustine in the valley of Franconia, his fellow philosopher, greetings.

I would rejoice to answer your letters, as Christ may make me rejoice; and I would send the volumes you requested, if at last I had them. For I have been zealous with a good zeal for the very great and very weighty hidden investigators of nature, the zeal which the most ancient philosophers possessed. Yet I give you thanks beyond what mortals can repay, my sweetest brother, since you have kept the bond of mutual affection inviolate. For in this familiar matter, which you seem to have managed most diligently with grave modesty, I have plainly recognized this; I praise the deed, and I give thanks that will never die. And so I would very much like to comply with your requests, if I had what you ask for, as Christ knows. I recently saw various Latin translations of Ficino; I have read many most brilliant volumes of Pico della Mirandola, that most excellent man.

Steganography

I saw Hippolytus in Greek; whether he has been translated at all, I do not know. The highest Truth, Christ, to whom no shadows conceal anything, knows that from my heart I desire to comply with your request. I beg you, be zealous for virtue with the zeal of righteousness; despise praises and honors that will perish. Consider true praise to be the imitation of Christ going before us. See to it, I beg you, that as a priest you may exist in works, and love Christ for all the time in which you live. A true lover of Christ burns with zeal for justice. True repose of the soul, knowledge of the savior, and pious observance of Catholic tradition prepare the eternal glory of all. May glorious Jesus Christ, giver of all good things, grant you the love of eternity, making you a Catholic priest of Christians. Farewell. 4 Kalends of April, in the year 1500.

When the person to whom the letters have been sent has received them, being skilled in the art, after first performing the things that are generally customarily done beforehand, let him arrange the lord of the ascendant with the others that are customarily placed on the little chart, and let him say the prescribed conjuration. When it has been said, the spirit who was sent will appear visibly; turning to him, let him say fearlessly: Fabelmerufyn passoriel liertos ryneas melchus thyrmo nydran vear padroys. When this song has been completed, the spirit will at once approach gently and will faithfully disclose the entrusted mystery.

But everyone who is going to operate in this art must take care, both the one who sends the spirit and the one to whom he has been destined, not to presume to perform anything in public or among others who are not skilled in this art, because all the hourly spirits love secrecy and detest publicity; and they would not depart without danger.

Their office is general for all things; and they are sufficiently ready and benevolent in all matters whatsoever have been entrusted to them, faithful and secure; nor are they unwilling in obedience. But when summoned in public, they do not depart without harm or danger to the one summoning them.

Whatever the Secret May Be.

Whatever the secret may be that you have, and that must be entrusted to an absent friend, entrust it neither to letters, lest they be read by anyone, nor to a courier, lest by some occasion, or corrupted by a price or by fear, he betray you publicly. Call the spirit appointed to the hour, entrust the secret to him, fearing nothing: he will carry it faithfully.

STEGANOGRAPHY

He will form letters at will.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Arnold Bostius, Carmelite of Ghent, his fellow philosopher: greeting and charity.

Since I have known you as a lover of humane arts, a devout worshipper of the Christian faith, and a very great supporter of all philosophers, I gladly oblige your requests, moved by the wonderful pleasure of friendship. Behold, at your urging I send to you the book previously noted, concerning ecclesiastical writers and Catholic doctors, so that you may have something with which to delight your mind. But send back to me the codices of Hermes, the books of Dionysius on spirits, and the great work of Puenclus on winter [questions]. May Christ deign to adorn the eyes of our heart with the most fervent zeal of his love; and may he cause us to have love for heavenly goods, and, stripped of desires for the lowest things, may he teach us to despise vain honors, so that we may be able to penetrate the sublime matters of the art and also the great secrets of nature, and may have a continual desire for philosophy, to purify our affections, by which we may always adorn the Catholic faith with most honorable morals. Hold fast the great saying: you are a philosopher; give up everything and you will find it. Regard the hour of death as near, at which may you, prepared, meet what you attempt. Farewell. 3 Kal. Apr. 1500.

When you have received any letters sealed with the character of Vequaniel, write on a new schedule the figure of the lord of the ascendant and of the twelfth house, with the other things that are required for the art, and on its back the aforesaid conjuration; and immediately the spirit sent will appear visibly. Keep everything that we prescribe to you, and you will make great progress in this science.

Procedure for a Secret Messenger

Let there be any secret, great and very hidden, which you wish absolutely no one to know except one person. Summon as many spirits appointed to the hour as you wish, and entrust the secret to the chief one. Write letters,

in whatever form you wish, in which nothing secret is contained and which need fear no one’s inspection at all.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, to Rutger Vencaius the Sicambrian, Canon of the Order of the divine father Augustine of the monastery of Damentis, greetings.

Those matters which he proposed to me to be solved, with Christ’s help I have resolved. Whether well, you who proposed them must decide. I shall briefly report to you what happened, or rather a summary. A certain brother recently reported to me, and also a friend, not the least of men, that a young man had been raised from the dead at the invocation of Christ, reporting wondrous and dreadful things among the dead, and narrating the torments of wicked Christians, namely of those who by acting perversely crucified Christ. They are especially guilty of this: that, forgetful of the most gracious benefit of redemption, they always remained ungrateful to Christ. He said that they suffer horrible things, those who were known to be ungrateful for his benefits by not living well, and who, blinded by sin, neglected future joys while pursuing the pleasures of the world; and that, in the bitterest way for the negligences they had committed, they cried out: “Deservedly we endure these things, we who were always ungrateful to the redeemer of the human race. We were Christians in name, Gentiles in action. Wretched as we are, we always sought earthly consolations; therefore we receive the due recompense of eternal damnation. Alas, most unhappy that we are, why did we offend Christ? Why did we despise the time granted to us?”

The resurrected young man reported many other things to us, which I am now wholly unable to write, being especially hindered by serious business. Therefore, brother, let us zealously imitate the footsteps of Christ, always giving thanks to our most gentle Savior, and praying that he may pardon the guilt we have committed. Farewell. 3 Kalends of April.

When the one skilled in the art has received the letters sent to him, let him observe the lord of the ascendant of that same hour and the sign of the twelfth house, and let him write their characters, with the rest, on paper, together with the other things required for the operation. When these have been said, the spirit that was sent will approach and will faithfully and without danger reveal the secret entrusted to him.

And it should be noted that the dukes are rarely called in the fifth hour for the operations of Steganography, because they are not always necessary, since the counts, together with the servants assigned to them, are abundantly sufficient for us for every operation. Yet if anyone should wish to see some of the dukes also, and to make use of their power, he may call one, two, or more; and they will come without delay, for they are sufficiently well disposed and ready to obey those who operate.

96 STEGANOGRAPHY: An Argument for Announcing a Secret.

Let there be any sort of secret of ours for a friend, which we want no one besides him to know; and let it be of such a kind that it is not safely entrusted either to letters or to messengers. Let us call one of the counts of Sasquiel named above; let us entrust the secret to him; let us add letters sealed with his character; and we shall be safe.

The Tenor of the Letter, as Desired.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to the religious brother Nicolaus Baselius of Durckheim, monk of Hirsau, greetings.

Good brother, you neglect holy obedience and humility; you undermine the constitutions of Benedict. By the report of all who have come successively, I have learned that you hate good zeal, despise the norm of religion and Catholic obedience, and occupy yourself with secular works and arts. Good brother, what is being done? You have disturbed us, and you are zealous for foolish and double-tongued men; you love hatred, bitterness, quarrels, and contentions; you hate goodness; you are double-tongued, contentious, and proud. Fool, what are you doing? The time is at hand to correct these negligences of yours more quickly, according to justice and zealously; and unless you hasten humbly to us, to break the zeal of bitterness with the lashes of humiliations, we are compelled by our office to be zealous against everything that is seditious toward the purity of faith and Catholic morals. Farewell from Sponheim, the day before the Kalends of April, in the year 1500.

When the person skilled in the art to whom the letters are sent has received them, after recognizing the character of Sasquiel and after the usual things have first been done and are to be done, let him say the above-mentioned conjuration; and immediately the spirit who was sent will appear and present himself visibly. When he has been seen, let him at once say these words: Fabelmerusyn aueual vearyan cralti penason. When the spirit has heard these words, he will at once approach and reveal the secret.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, sends greetings to the brave knight Heinrich von Bunan, his most studious fellow philosopher.

I had lent you my books on condition that they be returned, dearest knight Bunan; but behold, you have by no means returned those which you ought to have sent back shortly. You act against the law which the Catholic faith has sanctioned concerning a promise: do not delay,

Of Steganography

through slowness, to discharge what you promised. It is not fitting for a good and honorable man, born of noble parents and ancestors, to violate a promise. He had promised to return them very diligently in a short time. It is a mark of fickleness to postpone a promise, as it were, to the Greek Kalends. Have I not waited long enough with great goodwill? To promise the greatest things and to repay the smallest is most shameful. Good faith adorns a soldier. What more serious fault is there than to deny the loan that was promised? Nor does it befit a Christian to be unwilling to observe an agreement. The constitution of Christian law commands one to keep a promise, to repay a loan, and willingly to do also for others what you desire to be done for you. I demand back my books, which I had lent to you when you begged for them. Set aside the longer excuses which you promise until the Greek Kalends. You keep my mind attentive with brief delays. Consider your honorable name and the noble family of the Bunans, and send me back my volumes. Farewell from Sponheim, April 2, in the year of the Lord 1500.

Mefarym burne theor alueas casuean cralti lierto aply charmoyS.

Subject of the Secret at Will

Let us have any secret whatever, which we wish to write to a friend far absent, and of such a kind that we do not wish it to come to the knowledge of anyone else, as can often happen. Therefore, lest either the letter-carrier reveal the mystery for any reason, or the letter come into foreign hands, let us work, and through the spirit we shall be secure.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, sends greetings to Lord Conrad, Abbot of Saint Stephen at Wuerzburg.

A rumor has gone out about the abbey of Limburg, that it has dismissed Brother Johannes Feilsdorf, a faithful man and especially skilled in temporal affairs,

and has introduced new monks from Pantimorum and appointed them its officers. I am greatly astonished at this useless deed. Yet when I recall the custom of the men of Limburg, I do not know what to say. Indeed I see men ignorant of temporal affairs, who dismissed a faithful man because he rebuked their actions. They ought to have given thanks to our Savior Jesus Christ for the fidelity of so great a brother, who could have disclosed their necessities. Wretches, why do you reject a good and necessary helper? What shall I say? I do not praise the departure of so useful a brother, one most skilled in temporal affairs, who would very quickly have assisted the men of Limburg. I grieve greatly that the monks of Limburg have so lost their sense, who dismissed an excellent man and appointed as stewards monks who are worth absolutely nothing in temporal affairs. Macharius, abbot, it did not befit a man to act so. First you praised him; now you have rejected a man very necessary to you, to be put after no one. I confess that, if Christ had given him to me, as befits a Christian I would now give the greatest thanks and would take care that he never departed. But you, ungrateful to Christ, preferred to dismiss a faithful man, wearied by your counsel, lest, with your affairs abandoned, there should seem to be hope of recovery. From Sponheim, 3 Nones of April, 1500.

When these letters, or any others, have been received by the one to whom they are sent, marked with the sign of Osmadael, let the person skilled in the art, after first setting out what must be set out beforehand, say the prescribed conjuration; and soon the spirit sent will appear visibly. When you have seen him, say: Menason aproysy elmano thulneas assierto mauear veneas cralnoti permason. When these words have been spoken, the messenger spirit will disclose the secret to you.

John Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, to the religious father John Hugo, guardian of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis in Kreuznach: greeting and charity.

Religious and venerable father, know that you freely grant to friends all things suited to them. Therefore I humbly beg that, in view of Catholic piety, you not take it badly that your zealous brothers have been kept with us rather long, with the greatest charity; for it was necessary, at my request, that they remain. Their glorious joy was a delight to us, as we all rejoiced without fault. We exulted in the Lord with spiritual joy, giving thanks to almighty God with good zeal. What gathering, I ask, is more religious than such a one? Where nothing idle is said, nothing wicked is pursued. May Christ Jesus, savior of all, make them rejoice in everlasting glory. Glorious lovers of the virtues place nothing before truth. We rejoiced with holy joy, praying that you receive the aforesaid brothers peacefully and put aside every zeal of bitterness. Farewell. From Sponheim, 3 Nones of April, in the year of the Lord 1500.

Establishment of the Secret.

Let there be a friend of ours, whose good we favor; we fear that he is to be supplanted and deceived by some roaming impostor. We therefore wish him to be advised. We cannot do it by open words through messengers; by letters, lest they fall into someone’s hands, we likewise dare not. Therefore, so that we may be safe and our secret may always remain hidden, let us call at least one spirit, a duke of those named above. He comes, obeys, and faithfully carries the message.

166 OF THE STEGANOGRAPHY

Let the letter be composed as one pleases.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Spanheim, to Heinrich of Banau, gilded knight, distinguished philosopher and mathematician, sends greeting.

Since you are most devoted to the study of the liberal arts, you will rejoice exceedingly, I think, that you have found a new companion in studies. The man who will deliver this letter to you is a man of great knowledge, a supreme philosopher, a most subtle arithmetician, a most eloquent rhetorician, and a most profound mathematician, and in every way most excellently learned. He speaks most elegantly, shining with Ciceronian eloquence. If you were not especially my friend, I would have kept so great a man entirely for myself, since through experience of him I found him to be a most learned philosopher. I favor you greatly; receive with gratitude the philosopher whom I send to you, moved by singular affection. O that all our students were such, who with fearful heart despise noble knowledge! That man continually studies philosophy and the other sciences, and the loftiest depths of nature; he treats them constantly and penetrates them most acutely. Therefore remember, Heinrich Bunau, for Christ’s sake, to deal with the man with a generous countenance. Farewell from Spanheim, 2 November, in the year of the Lord 1500.

When the friend to whom the letter is sent has received it, being skilled in this science of Steganography, let him do everything that must be done according to the art, and let him add the prescribed conjuration, as is customary. And when he has seen the spirit sent present, let him say these words to him, as to the more powerful among the spirits: Camyn aparsy aslotiel omeat reneas vean triamy cralty penafon. When these have been uttered, the spirit will immediately come nearer and will reveal the secret to him.

The Establishment of Any Secret Whatever.

We have a secret for a friend, or for anyone else skilled in our art, which we cannot signify either by letters or by messenger, because we fear danger in both cases. Therefore we call a spirit; we entrust the secret to the superior one, and in all things we are safe.

The tenor of the letters, at pleasure.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, to brother Quirinus, a monk of Corbie in France, greetings.

Concerning the mother of the perpetual Virgin Mary I send my prayer, which you recently requested, Quirinus: Hail, most kindly mother Anna, most radiant parent of the Virgin Mary; you most peaceful helper of all the innocent; you noble refuge of those who seek you; quiet blessing of holiness. Hail, most gentle advocate of the poor, most beautiful comforter of those who groan, most adorned storehouse of virtues. Hail, happy refresher of the sorrowful, most health-giving medicine of the sick, and most renowned promoter of faithful Christians. Obtain pardon for us who pray; appease the dread judge Christ; intercede for your servants, that they may attain blessedness. With you interceding, we ask that he receive us wretched ones by his kindness. Amen. 8 Ides of April, in the year of the Lord 1500.

When the one to whom the letters are sent has received them, being skilled in the art, let him first attend to the character of the hour attached to the letter. Then let him append the prescribed prayer in the manner and order required; and soon the spirits sent will appear. When these words have been spoken to the spirit superior among the others, who is easily recognized by his habit and crown and always precedes the others, he will at once reveal the secret in the ear.

An argument for any secret whatsoever, as desired, that presents itself.

We have a friend far away; we know that a danger threatens him, of which he is unaware. We wish to warn him, but for certain reasons we do not dare do so openly. Therefore, according to the hour, we summon the spirits appointed for this operation and safely entrust the secret to them.

Letters, composed as desired, we seal with the spirit’s sign.

No one who boasts of temporal things is at all to be called virtuous; and one who loves transitory things cannot be a lover of Justice, for Catholic integrity detests a person who gapes after desires. For the holy religion of the Christian faith forbids love of the world to its people, since whoever loves worldly joys loses heavenly happiness. A Catholic who does not live in a Catholic manner is shown to have denied Christ; and one who loves temporal things is not said to be a good Catholic. Whoever loves the Creator seeks the joys of spiritual things. The lover of Christ despises all the pleasures of the world and does not care for unstable glory and riches. But the lover of the world hates virtues and cares nothing for future joys. Alas, what are you doing, Christians, intent on vain things? You think things that are not honorable, and you do things contrary to religion. Do not, wretches, I beseech you, do not love the soon-perishing vanities of this world. Take care rather to love Christ, that he may receive us into the heavenly kingdoms.

When one skilled in the art has received this prescribed little prayer, or any others, sealed with the character of Berathiel, let him diligently do everything prescribed in the art, and let him say the conjuration. And when he has seen that the spirits, who will come without delay, are present, let him say to the chief one, who walks crowned: Famerusyn melysno alny vemoby dreary drymes charsony. When these words have been said, he will come nearer [unclear]

Let the tenor of the letter be as desired.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Brother Nicolaus Basselius, monk of Hirsau, with greeting, says that he should present this prayer.

Almighty God, exalted Creator of all things, who through Christ redeemed us Christians, gave Catholics the zeal of his love, and through the light of faith made known the remission of sins to believers. Moreover, he most generously gave his beloved Son, the gracious light, to free all of us believers from the power of the enclosed Tartarean king, and to destroy the dark prison and most cruel Zabulus. What, as Christians, can we worthily render for the passions of Christ, weak men, professing the Catholic faith without works of righteousness? Therefore, praying most devoutly to you, we praise our Redeemer with the highest praises, saying: praise be to you, eternal light, most kindly Savior of all, who redeemed us by your blood. Jesus Savior, look upon our frailty, and pour into our hearts the zeal of the Catholic faith. Holy is your zeal; it works compunction in the hearts of those seeking you, Christ most kindly Savior. O eternal light, sweetest Jesus, illumine the darkness of your servant with your accustomed goodness. Jesus, eternal Savior, save our souls; may you grant us eternal joys. Christ, hear your humble servants, most unworthy of all. Grant us, who humbly ask, a good zeal. Amen.

We wrote on the 18th day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord 1500.

Let the secret be whatever occurs to us, great and difficult.

The secret which we wish to communicate to a friend through the spirits may be whatever occurs to us according to the occasion and the variety of business, provided that it is not trivial, and such as can otherwise safely be entrusted.

Johannes Trithemius, to the nuns on the Mount of Saint Rupert, adorning the Catholic faith with shining virginity, sends the wish that they may continually merit eternal happiness by the most holy zeal of religion.

By the mercy of the eternal King, we prudently send to you the man long awaited, greatly experienced in temporal affairs, Johannes, native of Raunenstat, for a long time the reverend and zealous abbot of the monastery of Vilsdorf, who freely resigned that abbey. On account of him, as I had promised you, I went to the monastery of Lüneburg, where he was serving Christ, occupied in continual prayers and readings of the holy scriptures with the monks of that monastery; and I asked him to come down to your convent, to take up the care of temporal affairs, and to become procurator and cellarer, since the Abbot of Limburg, with his usual instability, had changed his mind.

I was able to obtain consent from him to release him. At last, with Christ inspiring him, he consented, though timidly, because he fears to serve nuns, who are changed very easily. He does not fear without reason, since, as experience has taught us, nuns have sometimes given their stewards a reward not praiseworthy for benefits received. A woman’s mind is found to be changed by the zeal of bitterness.

But with Christ granting it, I know that he will be useful to you. He is a Christian; he is a monk; he fears the Savior; and he is of good understanding. Therefore accustom yourselves to restrain feminine changeability, so that you remember to be constant: receive him with holy honor and sincere charity, laying aside every levity of womanly spirit, especially since, with the help of Christ the Redeemer, who cherishes charity, he can help you and restore the condition of temporal affairs in your monastery, which has collapsed. Farewell. From Spanheim, 17 Kalends of May, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1500.

When the person to whom the letters marked with the character of Tartys are sent has received them, being skilled in our art, let him observe the lord of the ascendant and do, most diligently, all and each of the things that must be done, and let him add the usual conjuration. And when he has said these words with strong intention to the principal leader, he will at once approach calmly and reveal the secret.

CHAPTER XV.

Whose hour is called Quabron, and its supreme angel is called Serquanich, having under his command many princes, dukes, counts, and servants without number.

The third hour of the night is called Quabron. Its emperor and supreme angel is Serquanich, having under his command many princes, dukes, and counts in twelve orders, with a great continuous division of servants. For in the first order there are 10; in the second, 20; in the third, 30; in the fourth, 40; in the fifth, 50; in the sixth, 60; in the seventh, 70; in the eighth, 80; in the ninth, 90; in the tenth, 100; in the eleventh, 1,000; in the twelfth, 10,000. The Second Book

I have made a large Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers, which I recently presented to your fraternity to be examined. Since I brought it to conclusion too hastily, I admit that I passed over some very famous men, not because I grudged their name the benefit of the catalogue, as a swollen critic accuses, attacking the catalogue with the stupidest words. He thought that I had failed to mention his people solely out of envy, which is utterly false. Indeed, I wrote and affirmed that the conception of the most holy Mother of God was always most beautiful, without any blemish of original transgression. This the swollen critic, wishing to rebuke swollenly, said, with the emptiest rashness against Catholic observance, that the most radiant Virgin had been stained by the guilt of original fault. It is rash to wish to defile the most blessed Virgin. But the most renowned doctors of Cologne, wishing to root out the mad little brother’s opinion, which was contrary to the truth, summoned him and compelled him to retract his empty tales. They asserted and also confirmed by statute that the most blessed Virgin must be believed to have been most pure, and at no time, however brief, to have been subject to original defilement. I wanted to write these things to you, since you love the truth, so that you may avoid those who reproach the most blessed Virgin. Farewell. 16 Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord 1500.

The secret, whatever occurs to you at the time, which you wish someone absent to know in this fourth hour of the night, you may safely entrust to the spirits, provided it is of such a kind that you cannot safely disclose it to him either by letters or by messengers. For those things that we can disclose without danger either by letters or by messengers we must by no means disclose through the ministry of spirits. To the venerable father in Christ, the steward of the Limburgers, the religious lord called Johannes Westdorffen, Johannes Ovilis, humble abbot of Sponheim, sends the joys of heaven.

The nuns of Saint Rupert long most eagerly for you as their governor, and with humble goodwill ask you to undertake the administration of the temporal affairs of that monastery. To serve the devout virgins of Christ is praiseworthy and meritorious. You have as the excellent visitor of the spiritual affairs of that named monastery, embracing you with the greatest honor, a man grave in character, adorned with virtues, cautious in counsel, beloved by all, of good reputation for the conduct of monastic religion, and notable among all people, whose life is deservedly most pleasing to Christ: the excellent abbot of the monastery of Saint John. He is most learned, most studious, and most skilled in the writings both of Christians and of gentiles, and he far and notably surpasses the wisdom of all people. He knows very well how to govern the flock entrusted to him, and he is a zealous guardian of the virgins of Christ, whose enclosure he preserves most firmly. Do not be afraid to serve under him such honorable nuns, for he knows how to govern the brides of Christ according to the monastic law with the best discretion, and by virtue and zeal for the Christian faith he will gladly assist you in necessity. Since you have as a familiar friend so illustrious and kindly a pastor, I ask that you gladly take up the helm of government of such religious virgins. The spouse, guardian, and most kindly rewarder of the nuns will repay your labor and theirs with eternal joys.

May he grant you, with good zeal, to be zealous for better things. Farewell from Sponheim, 18 May, in the year 1500.

Whatever secret you have, which otherwise you cannot safely make known to a friend living far away or nearby, entrust it, with the rite and form required according to the art, to the more powerful one among the spirits, fearing nothing, because they are well-disposed and faithful.

Let the letters be formed at pleasure.

The Catholic faith saves no one who despises the ardor of divine love. To believe and not to have zeal for divine love contributes nothing at all to the soul’s redemption. Many people are now found boasting in the Catholic faith, but few have the works of the Christian faith; idle faith dies. Many believe, but very few observe God’s commandments. Alas, how weak is the zeal of believing which even unbelieving people can have more strongly, and many do have it. The Gentiles and those people who do not believe that our savior became man, the son of the almighty, will be tormented by the punishments of hell.

But all those who believe that the Son of God came into the world and accomplished the zeal of human redemption by his murder will be exercised with heavier punishments, if they do not adorn the Christian faith with holy works, and, always entangled in sins, prefer the honors of the world to eternal blessedness, pursuing impious actions with zeal and staining the purity of faith by private morals contrary to obedience. But lovers of God, who have the right zeal of the Christian faith, prefer nothing to God, imitate Christ, flee sins, and despise riches and honors. Now therefore, you who glory in faith, attend to these words: love God, and you will have the reward of blessedness by pursuing justice with zeal. If you love the vanities of the world contrary to the honor of God, you will receive the reward of those who pursue iniquity with zeal: the horrors of hell. Written on the 15th day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord 1500.

Remember your promise, which you made when, receiving the Catholic faith in Christ, you offered it with a solemn vow to eternal joy; for to those who despise the temporal pleasures and delights of the present life in view of the future eternal rest, eternal joy is without doubt promised. He who has faith, but neglects to have divine love, is faithless, and presumes in vain concerning faith also. The creator, reformer, and maker of all things created the first man, Adam, to whom he joined a most beautiful wife named Eve, the mother of all living, prefiguring the Catholic Church, to be joined to pastors, shining beautifully with upright morals, and to bear as sons men of good works, who through humility receive the kingdoms of heaven that will endure without end.

Christ redeemed us through his kindness, humbling himself for our sake. Howl, mortals, you who now laugh, and who in many ways have most ungratefully despised the kindness of our glorious redeemer by very grave sins and dreadful crimes. Behold, the Turk, the deadly enemy of Christians, will move his army from Hungary and will slaughter men like beasts. The savage one has crossed the Danube, inflamed as if by fire with zeal for impiety. Therefore mourn, most wretched people, destined to die in a dreadful slaughter; you will die in bitter zeal, because your offenses will overtake you. You have despised the laws of God, your most kind redeemer. We have heard how cruelly the Turk has invaded Hungary, Bohemia, and Poland: he has destroyed very strong cities; women and virgins consecrated to God, keeping chastity in zeal for holiness, he has most shamefully violated, horribly slaughtering Catholics of every kind, ranging everywhere like cruel beasts. You will feel his horrible cruelty in a short time: for he will suddenly trouble Germany with his most warlike army, unless a general defense by the princes resists him without delay. Therefore, groaning, take up humility; amend your ways; pray to God with tears that he may grant you remission of your offenses and free us from the enemies who thirst greatly for our blood. I wrote this on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord 1500. Johannes Trithemius.
